<p><strong>Its fourth inward level:</strong> what is attributed to concrete existence, assigned to the reality of humanity, delimited by it and revealing its properties within the ranks of the cosmos as spirit, imaginal form, and sensible form. This is the inward level alluded to in the words “I become his hearing, his sight, his tongue, and his hand.”</p>
<p><strong>Its fifth inward level:</strong> what is attributed to the heart, which receives the self-disclosure of inward existence within it, alluded to in the saying “The heart of My servant encompasses Me.”</p>
<p><strong>Its sixth inward level:</strong> what is attributed to the comprehensive, merciful, undelimited existence appearing at the second intermediary rank through its overflowing generosity, which extends to all things.</p>
<p><strong>Its seventh inward level:</strong> these very meanings that are at the first rank, united in reality though possessing distinguishable relative judgments.</p>
<p>Each of these meanings—speech, hearing, sight, and power—has a special effect and judgment at each rank. Its absence from a human person at a given rank renders that person mute, deaf, blind, or weak at that rank. From this one may understand the Qurʾānic statement, “Deaf, dumb, and blind: they do not return” (2:18): that is, from the world to the hereafter, or from the first inward level to the second. At the first level they did hear, see, and speak.</p>
<p>People are at different degrees concerning the opening of the gates of these inward levels. Some have no gate opened at all, such as the insane and infants. Some have only the first gate opened: such is the person who has received good in this world but has no portion in the hereafter. Others have the second opened, namely the ordinary members of the people of Islam and faith.</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p28" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p28"><h3 id="title-b2007-p28">B2007 p. 28 · The roots of the divine attributes and the seventh gate</h3>

<p>Others have the third gate opened: these are the elect among the believers. Others have the fourth: these are at the beginning of the station of sainthood (<em>walāya</em>) and spiritual excellence (<em>iḥsān</em>). Those to whom the fifth is opened are among the intermediates. Those to whom the sixth is opened are among the people of the final stations, the perfected and the singular ones. Not even a small aperture of the seventh gate is opened to anyone except the possessor of the Muhammadan inheritance, for the seventh inward degree is particularly his—may God bless him and grant him peace.</p>
<p>Now the first self-disclosure, insofar as it includes the inward speech and informing described earlier, contains a perfection attributed to it and to its considerations, together with a comprehensive and undifferentiated awareness of that perfection. This is the origin and inward reality of life and of the Living.</p>
<p>Insofar as it involves contemplation, it contains an awareness of the diffusion of that perfection throughout the details of the considerations of oneness: this is the origin and inward reality of knowledge and the Knowing.</p>
<p>Insofar as it involves the inclination to hearing and attentive listening, it entails a consideration that is the origin of will.</p>
<p>Insofar as it involves the effect produced by that unitary discourse within itself, from which the disclosure and finding ensued, it includes a particular orientation of efficacy toward actualizing name-related perfection, removing its impediments, and obtaining its conditions, without introducing otherness. The effective judgment of that particular orientation is the inward reality of power. Its effect of realizing perfection in detail and obtaining its conditions contains the reality of generosity, through the overflowing bestowal of existence upon the reality of each existent. This belongs to the conditions for name-related perfection in detail.</p>
<p>The intermediary character of the first determination, which establishes these considerations, and its receptivity to the first self-disclosure, entails and determines the reality of justice and equitable proportioning. To it belong the assignment of all ranks and the preservation of justice among receptive possibilities between necessity and impossibility.</p>
<p>The seventh inward degree of speech, hearing, sight, and power—each identical with the Essence and with the others under that consideration—is therefore the generative principle of life and the Living; knowledge and the Knowing; and equitable proportioning and the Equitable. Considered as realized at the core of the second intermediacy, the comprehensive aspect includes each of them in all the others, with a hidden trace of their distinction. Yet the whole is a single reality at the first determination, the first rank of the most holy Essence, and the first rank of knowledge insofar as knowledge is the Essence itself, not an attribute or qualification additional to it.</p>
<p>Some of the great masters, considering this intermediary character, call it <strong>the Reality of Realities</strong> (<em>ḥaqīqat al-ḥaqāʾiq</em>) because it is universal and is the origin of every consideration—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p29" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p29"><h3 id="title-b2007-p29">B2007 p. 29 · The supreme intermediary and two kinds of perfection</h3>

<p>—and determination, the inward reality of every divine and cosmic reality, and the source from which each arises, permeating it in its entirety so that it is divine in divine realities and cosmic in cosmic realities. All are its manifestations and the forms of its articulated details. Some call it the <strong>Supreme Intermediary</strong> (<em>al-barzakh al-akbar</em>), which comprehends all intermediary states and is the origin pervading them.</p>
<p>Revelation alludes to it through the station of “or nearer” (<em>aw adnā</em>), which is the inward reality of “the distance of two bows” (<em>qāb qawsayn</em>): that is, the nearness of the two bows of unity and multiplicity, or of receptivity and activity, or of necessity and possibility. The two are gathered together as one continuous circle, though in this station a hidden trace of distinction and multiplication remains between them. The inward reality of that station is “or nearer” than the two bows: here no trace of distinction or plurality remains within the encompassing circle between the judgment of unicity and that of oneness.</p>
<p>Some call this the <strong>Aḥmadian Reality</strong>, established in the exact centre of intermediacy and equitable equilibrium, such that no one name or attribute predominates over it. The first self-disclosure determined in and by the first determination is its light, making its rank manifest; the appearance of that light is appointed within the comprehensive intermediary reality. The Prophet's purified and Godwary heart is the form of this determination and intermediacy—not a bodily form, but a comprehensive intelligible one. His noblest elemental temperament, realizing the highest degree of equilibrium, is its corporeal image and manifestation.</p>
<p>That first luminous self-disclosure, as we have said, is thus his light in the first instance—may God bless him and grant him peace—as alluded to in the saying, “The first thing God created was my light.” God speaks the truth and guides to the path.</p>
<p><strong>Chapter.</strong> The first self-disclosure just described contains <em>perfection</em>, whose reality is that what ought to be obtained is obtained in the manner in which it ought to be obtained. This falls into two divisions. The first is an essential, comprehensive, unitary perfection, realized in the first rank. At the beginning of the second rank, life and the name <em>the Living</em> become determined, as will be explained if God wills.</p>
<p>Essential self-sufficiency accompanies this perfection. Its meaning is that the Essence witnesses and apprehends itself under the consideration of its oneness together with all its considerations, affairs, and states; with all its intelligible, spiritual, imaginal and sensory forms and manifestations; and with their principles and concomitants, some included within others, some determined and branching from others as roots and branches, genera, species, and individuals, first coming-forth and return, descent and ascent, this world, the intermediate state, and the next. Their possessors witness and apprehend these at the cosmic ranks either together or in succession, as distinct things relative—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p30" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p30"><h3 id="title-b2007-p30">B2007 p. 30 · Essential and name-related perfection</h3>

<p>—to their apprehension of distinct things within their particular ranks and their restriction by those ranks; but all are a single reality relative to the witnessing of the One, the One-in-Unicity, in the ranks attributed to Him. This is detailed witnessing within a comprehensive whole, in a single act, as when a person graced with unveiling perceives innumerable palm trees and fruits within a single date-stone.</p>
<p>The <strong>second kind of perfection</strong> is the differentiated perfection through the divine names (<em>al-kamāl al-asmāʾī al-mufaṣṣal</em>), extending through the particulars of the names and realities. It is what appears to the Essence when its considerations and the realities of their differentiation are considered in detail, as attributed to particular ranks. It therefore takes place <strong>on condition of something—indeed, of several things</strong>: determination, what is other, a relative otherness, a locus of manifestation, gathering together, an intelligible or formal composition, and other such conditions. Essential perfection, by contrast, is realized without condition of anything at all.</p>
<p>The reality of name-related perfection is that the Essence appears to itself under the consideration of its totality and comprehensive unity: its affairs, considerations and loci of manifestation appear in detail, or comprehensively following their differentiation, as things other than one another. This witnessing, however, must be through a locus displaying a universal affair that comprehends all its individuals in actuality—namely, the <strong>true Perfect Human</strong>. Thus the Essence finds itself through that perfect locus.</p>
<p>It also appears to itself through each distinguished individual among the loci of manifestation of those affairs. Each individual becomes manifest and finds itself and its like, insofar as they are named “others” and restricted by particular ranks.</p>
<p>Consider now <strong>knowledge</strong>, whose reality is the appearance of the very reality of a thing, such that the effect of what appears is obtained in the one to whom it appears, precisely in respect of that appearance. Consider <strong>existence</strong>, whose reality is what enables a thing to find itself in itself, in another, or to find another in another, whether in a locus, a rank, or the like. Consider <strong>light</strong>, which discloses what is concealed, and <strong>witnessing</strong>, which is presence together with what is witnessed.</p>
<p>These all belong to the first self-disclosure and the considerations included within it, insofar as it is one, without difference between the disclosure and those considerations or between one consideration and another, under the aspect of essential perfection. There is no true distinction, except a faint relative distinction when this perfection appears under the name <strong>the Living</strong>, and no other.</p>
<p>But under the consideration of name-related perfection—which belongs to the other universal, original, derivative and particular names—distinction, a locus of manifestation, rank, and relative or actual otherness are among its conditions. The differentiation of all the things just mentioned is therefore established and necessary. It arises, however, <strong>according to the locus and what that locus requires</strong>, not according to the intrinsic realities of the considerations themselves. Understand: a locus has an inescapable effect and a decisive judgment upon what stands and is established within it, whether the locus is formal, as with containers, or intelligible, as with ranks. A container makes its contents follow its colour or its figure, whether round, square, or otherwise—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p31" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p31"><h3 id="title-b2007-p31">B2007 p. 31 · What existence means at the first and second ranks</h3>

<p>—just as the saying reminds us that the colour of water is the colour of its vessel. Similarly, ranks exercise determining judgments over those who inhabit them. The sensory rank requires that nothing appear within it except sensibly; the rank of spirit and that of imaginal form do likewise, each according to its own mode. Nothing appears in the cosmic ranks except what is creaturely, and nothing appears in the ranks of the Real except the Real. Reflect, and you will know a secret: none knows, witnesses, or sees the Real save the Real, or through Him. Hold this in mind and you will attain many mysteries.</p>
<p>Among these matters is that <strong>knowledge</strong>, considered under the first rank and first determination, is the Essence's own reality appearing to itself while the considerations of oneness are contained within it and established. Thus knowledge is related to <strong>one known thing</strong>. Linguistically, therefore, the word “to know” at the first rank takes one object: there the Essence knows only itself.</p>
<p>At the second rank, however, knowledge is the Essence appearing to itself together with its affairs, by means of the loci of manifestation of those affairs, which at that rank are called attributes and realities. Under this consideration the verb “to know” takes two objects: the Essence appears to itself as <strong>possessing life, knowledge, will, power, speech, generosity, and justice</strong>. Accordingly, knowledge at the culmination of the second rank, in respect of the things known there, has real multiplicity and an aggregate, relative unity.</p>
<p>Another matter concerns <em>existence</em> (<em>wujūd</em>). At the first rank existence is that through which the Essence finds itself in itself, with the considerations of oneness included within it: a comprehensive finding whose details are contained within it, one of which multiplicity, difference, otherness, and distinction are denied.</p>
<p>At the second rank, existence admits two modes. The first is <strong>insofar as this rank is a locus for the Real's outward manifestation</strong>. Under that consideration existence is what enables the Essence to find its own reality under the aspect of its manifestation, together with the manifestation of its form—named the outward aspect of the name <strong>al-Raḥmān</strong>—and the manifestation of the forms of its determinations, which are called the divine names. The reality of existence remains one, although relational multiplicity may correctly be attributed to it.</p>
<p>Existence thus possesses <strong>real unity and relational multiplicity</strong>. Every divine name is the outward aspect of existence, which is identical with the Essence, but existence considered as determined and restricted by a meaning, or one may say by an attribute. Take <strong>the Living</strong>: it is a name of manifest, determined existence, but its determination and restriction take place through the meaning of <em>life</em>.</p>
<p>If we consider the reality of existence itself and the very determination, it is identical with the Essence, so that its unity is real. If, however, we consider its restriction to that meaning, its distinction from other meanings, and its determination according to that meaning, it is different from what the other names signify. It thus possesses a multiplicity of <strong>relational determinations</strong>.</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p32" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p32"><h3 id="title-b2007-p32">B2007 p. 32 · Created existence and the incapacity of the first rank to manifest plurality</h3>

<p>The <strong>second mode of manifest existence</strong> is this rank insofar as it is the locus for the appearance of the cosmos, comprising the cosmic ranks that follow and emerge from the second rank, such as the ranks of spirits, imaginal forms, and sense. Everything that becomes determined as existence within these is necessarily called “creature” and “other.”</p>
<p>Here the meaning and reality of existence is that through which the form of each determination finds itself, and finds its like, as a spiritual, imaginal, or corporeal existent, manifesting at each rank according to the character and judgment of that rank. For what exists at the rank of spirits finds itself and its like only spiritually; what exists in the imaginal rank finds itself only as an imaginal form; and what exists among bodies finds itself and its like only as corporeal and sensible.</p>
<p>On this account <strong>bringing into existence and creating</strong> mean nothing other than that the Creator—exalted and holy—gives cosmic realities that through which they find themselves, by attributing to them a determination from Him. Through the portion so attributed, He makes their properties appear at each rank according to its nature and law.</p>
<p>Thus the efficacy involved in the differences among forms of existential determination, the manner in which they disclose the properties of their respective realities, and the application of the names “same” and “other” to them, belongs to the ranks that function as intelligible loci. These loci are matters and relations that are privative in themselves: they have no existence externally, nor do they possess external existence in their own right. Consider, then, how something non-existent can have an effect—even though its privation is only relative and under one consideration—in the very reality of existence and in what is existent in every respect. You will discover something wondrous beyond the reach of sound intellects and minds.</p>
<p><strong>Chapter.</strong> The unity from which the aforementioned unicity and oneness arose was, without the condition of anything else, the first determination and consideration of the most holy Essence, and its first rank. As you know, it was the very receptivity to which manifestation and hiddenness were equally related. Consequently, the judgment of pure unicity remained rooted in it and essential to it, to its receptivity to manifestation, and to its being the first rank of the Essence.</p>
<p>It therefore admitted only the <strong>first self-disclosure</strong>, the comprehensive character of essential perfection, its unity, and the negation of multiplicity, distinction, and otherness, while the relations and considerations of oneness remained included within it. It could not receive a self-disclosure admitting multiplicity, even relational multiplicity, nor could it receive the name-related perfection inseparable from such a self-disclosure, which was the ultimate goal of the original orientation.</p>
<p>That is because pure unicity necessarily belongs to this first determination and receptivity, while the realization of name-related perfection depends upon plurality, distinction, and the effect of difference and otherness.</p>
<p>Now original love, expressed by “I loved,” bore that first self-disclosure and impelled it to turn toward the realization of this detailed name-related perfection. Yet it did not find, for that orientation—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p33" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p33"><h3 id="title-b2007-p33">B2007 p. 33 · The second receptivity and the differentiation of the names</h3>

<p>—a locus capable of receiving what it sought. By the strength of that longing orientation and amorous inclination, the self-disclosure returned to its origin. It reverted to the state in which manifestation and hiddenness were equally related to it, except that the power of love caused the judgment of manifestation—which is called <strong>essential mercy</strong>, identical with the inward reality of the absolute existence indicated by “that I might be known”—to predominate over the judgment of non-manifestation. The latter, through its association with the reality of inwardness and concealment, is figuratively called the inward reality of anger, preceded and overcome by mercy.</p>
<p>The self-disclosure therefore appeared again, now determined toward this goal by the force of original love that necessarily belonged to and remained inwardly present within it. [The wording of a short transition in the digital Arabic requires print comparison.] It bore a new determination from among the relations of oneness, capable of realizing its final aim—<strong>name-related perfection</strong>. That determination is the <strong>second receptive principle</strong>, which comprehends the opposed judgments of comprehensiveness and unity on the one side and differentiation and plurality on the other. It is related to <em>wāḥidiyya</em> and occurs at the second rank of its determinations. The disclosure appeared in this determination.</p>
<p>The second receptive principle, which is the form of the second determination, became the form and shadow of the first receptive principle and the first self-disclosure. It contained the forms of the determinations of oneness and was both their recipient and their agent. This resembles an exhalation that becomes determined and issues from the inwardness of a speaker, just as the first determination and disclosure issued from the innermost hiddenness and nondelimitation. That disclosure carried from the hidden, unconditioned Presence a trace of the darkness of its Unseen and the nondelimitation of its pre-eternity, together with the unending determinations of its everlastingness.</p>
<p>Through this exhalation-like unfolding, the <strong>cosmic realities</strong> were differentiated and distinguished from their original comprehensiveness and unity. Receptivity is attributed to them, in relation to the second determination and its receptivity. The <strong>divine names</strong>, to which efficacy and action belong, were attributed to the reality of the second self-disclosure.</p>
<p>All these cosmic realities and divine names became images and shadows of the affairs and considerations included within oneness—comprehensive and unitary there at the first rank, but differentiated at this second determination, which is the second rank. They became established and fixed there, some as roots and genera, others as branches, species, and particular individuals arising from those roots, genera, branches, or species. Under the judgment of the second rank they differ from one another in one respect and not in another.</p>
<p>The outward aspect of eternal knowledge pertains to them all, encompassing each known reality exactly as it is, <strong>in accordance with the known thing, not in accordance with a limitation in knowledge itself</strong>. Thus the universals comprehended within, and arising from, this second determination and receptive principle are called <strong>universal ranks</strong>, inasmuch as they serve as loci for the establishment of the remaining realities and for the outward existential manifestation of those capable of appearing within them—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p34" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p34"><h3 id="title-b2007-p34">B2007 p. 34 · Why the second determination bears many names</h3>

<p>—and because of the Essence's efficacy within and through these ranks. Such are the rank of meanings, the rank of spirits, the rank of imaginal reality, the sensory rank, and the various equilibria within them. Within those are the composite things called generated beings, whose comprehending and differentiating rank is the human rank. In the same way, the universal determinations of the self-disclosure determined within this second determination and receptive principle, with respect to the divine names, are the <strong>seven names</strong> whose explanation will follow.</p>
<p><strong>Chapter.</strong> This second, breath-like determination bears numerous names according to the considerations established within it, although its own reality is one.</p>
<p>It is called <em>the rank of Divinity</em> (<em>martabat al-ulūhiyya</em>) because it is the origin and source of the appearance of determinations, the source of every perfection attributed to them, the point toward which their orientations are directed, and the place to which they return. The second self-disclosure appearing through and within this rank is also the origin, totality, and place of return of the divine names. It is accordingly called by the names <strong>Allāh</strong> and <strong>the Deity</strong> (<em>al-ilāh</em>), since all worshippers turn to this rank and its self-disclosure, which is their goal: hearts find rest in it through the amplitude of its mercy, and intellects are kept from intrusive discourse concerning it.</p>
<p>It is called <em>the world of meanings</em> (<em>ʿālam al-maʿānī</em>) because all universal and particular meanings are realized and differentiated within it from their origin through their middle to their end.</p>
<p>It is called <em>the Presence of Inscription</em> (<em>ḥaḍrat al-irtisām</em>) because it bears the impressed forms of the relative multiplicity attributed to the divine names and the real multiplicity attributed to the cosmos and its realities.</p>
<p>It is called <em>the Presence of Eternal Knowledge</em> (<em>ḥaḍrat al-ʿilm al-azalī</em>) because eternal knowledge—the second of its universal determinations, the first being life—relates to all the other determinations, however numerous, and encompasses them in unity and multiplicity, whether real or relational.</p>
<p>It is also called the <em>Cloud-like Presence</em> (<em>al-ḥaḍra al-ʿamāʾiyya</em>), considered as the intermediary between unity and multiplicity. This intermediacy comprehends the original universal realities capable of being attributed primarily to the Real and secondarily to the cosmos. They are differentiated as universal roots and genera, from which branches, species, and particulars emerge within that very intermediacy as differentiated realities.</p>
<p>It is called <em>the Reality of Perfected Humanity</em> (<em>al-ḥaqīqa al-insāniyya al-kamāliyya</em>) insofar as those original universal realities are included within this intermediacy, their distinct judgments still present there as a hidden trace.</p>
<p>It is called <em>the rank of possibility</em> (<em>martabat al-imkān</em>) because the known things to which eternal knowledge relates are distributed among what is necessary in its manifestation and realization through itself, what is impossible in itself in every universal or particular rank, and what stands between these two, being equally related to either.</p>
<p>And because the second determination is the image of the first determination, which was the first rank of the most holy Essence, it is called <strong>the second rank</strong>. Thus all these names designate this—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p35" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p35"><h3 id="title-b2007-p35">B2007 p. 35 · Unity and multiplicity of the second determination</h3>

<p>—the aforementioned <strong>second, breath-like determination</strong>. This determination, and what became determined by it and within it through the second self-disclosure—which is the outward aspect of existence, named the outward reality of the names <em>Allāh</em> and <em>al-Raḥmān</em>—possess all the aforementioned principles: unity, multiplicity, and an intermediary which both separates and comprehends the two.</p>
<p>As for its unity, that is attributed to the second self-disclosure, whose relationship to essential unicity is stronger and which is more properly and primarily the locus of its manifestation. Yet the effect of oneness pervades it. The result of the judgment of oneness pervading it is the derivation from it of the relational multiplicity of the names, both negative and affirmative. On the other hand, the effect of its more primary relationship to essential unicity, as its manifestation, is the negation and removal of judgments, relations, and considerations in its negative names.</p>
<p>Thus <strong>the Pre-eternal</strong> is He of whom having a beginning is denied; <strong>the Self-sufficient</strong> is He of whom dependence is entirely denied, both in the subsistence of perfection in Him and its appearance through Him; <strong>the Unique</strong> is He of whom any counterpart conjoined to His Essence is denied—equal, like, rival, peer, or similitude, as though there could be another existence set opposite His existence. <strong>The Odd [without a pair]</strong> is He of whom anything pairing His attributes with another of their kind is denied: for instance, an all-comprehensive life possessing every perfection, and opposed by neither deficiency, death nor passing away, attributed to another so as to make His perfect and comprehensive life one of a pair.</p>
<p><strong>The All-holy</strong> is He of whom blameworthy attributes are denied, such as injustice, lying, futility, impurity, frivolity, incapacity, and the like. <strong>Peace</strong> is He of whom contention among the manifestations of attributes is denied: anger does not contend when He is pleased, nor haste when He exercises forbearance, nor the will to revenge when He forgives—and conversely.</p>
<p><strong>The Supremely Transcendent</strong> is He of whom what is excluded in the Unique, All-holy, and Peace is likewise excluded; so too <strong>the Exalted</strong>. God says, “Glory be to God above what they associate [with Him]” and “Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they describe”; there are analogous negative names.</p>
<p>The side of <strong>multiplicity</strong> in this second determination, by contrast, manifests essential oneness, but with the effect of unicity pervading it. Its being a manifestation of oneness is the source of the plurality of divine and cosmic determinations, both principal and subordinate, established and distinguished within it, some by real distinction and others by relation.</p>
<p>The effect of unicity pervading it, however, is that every group of those many entities has an all-comprehensive unity that constitutes its origin and source—or, rather, its totality and point of return—or, again, its genus or species. The many entities are first included within that unity, second arise from it, and third return to it. The rank of that unity precedes the rank of the entities arising from it. An example of this—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p36" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p36"><h3 id="title-b2007-p36">B2007 p. 36 · Hierarchical unities and the human intermediary</h3>

<p>—unity is first the self-disclosure, then the name <em>Allāh</em> and <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, then the name <em>the Living</em>, then the other fundamental names to be discussed, God willing.</p>
<p>Among cosmic entities there is the reality of the Supreme Pen and its existence, then the reality of the Supreme Spirit and its existence, then the reality of Nature, then the reality of Body and its existence, until one reaches Adam, peace be upon him, in his reality and existence. Every one of these comprises the individuals and species branching out and arising from it and attributed to it, arranged and distinguished in relation to one another in eternal knowledge and concrete existence.</p>
<p>A second judgment, arising from the permeation of unicity within this manifestation of oneness, is that each individual of these genera, species, and particular things has within it a <strong>pure, inward unicity</strong> in which no other thing at all resembles or participates with it.</p>
<p>As for the intermediary (<em>barzakh</em>) that truly gives rise to these two extremes, first establishing and determining them and then comprehending them, it is the <strong>human reality</strong>. It has two considerations: in one the judgment of unity and comprehensiveness predominates; in the other the judgment of plurality and detailed articulation predominates.</p>
<p>Under the latter, differentiated consideration it is called the <strong>Cloud-like Presence</strong> (<em>al-ḥaḍra al-ʿamāʾiyya</em>). It comprises the seven original universal realities mentioned before. Some are included within others; some become determined and branch out from others. They are articulated and distinguished. The first of them in determination, and the most comprehensive in its judgment, is the reality of <strong>life</strong>, meaning receptivity to perfection encompassing every perfection appropriate to a thing, and awareness of that perfection in its comprehensive and universal aspect.</p>
<p><strong>The name the Living</strong> is the very source of perfection, comprehending every perfection appropriate to it according to its own reality and rank, together with general and comprehensive awareness in which the particulars are included. Since no universal or particular reality, original or derivative, is devoid of a perfection appropriate to itself, the name the Living comprehends all the names by virtue of the perfections they contain, while life comprehends all realities as a whole.</p>
<p>Knowledge is contained within life and derives from it. At this second rank, knowledge relates to differentiated known things that become distinct and manifest to their knower; life, however, is awareness of them collectively, and the articulated details are contained within that collective whole. In this respect, knowledge is therefore included in life. As for will, its meaning is the seeking of what is willed and inclining toward it, whether by specification, arrangement, bringing into manifestation or concealment—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p37" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p37"><h3 id="title-b2007-p37">B2007 p. 37 · The seven principal names and their mutual inclusion</h3>

<p>—<strong>the name the Willing</strong> determined by this reality is the one who seeks and inclines toward assigning a thing its particular judgment, effect, attribute, and a rank for the judgments belonging to that thing and others. The ultimate object of this seeking is the manifestation of perfection through the divine names. What it wills through that arrangement, specification, attribution, and judgment is precisely this manifestation, which belongs to the characteristics of knowledge. Consequently the Willing and will are included within knowledge and arise from it.</p>
<p>Speech, in its reality, is a breath arising from within the one who breathes, containing a meaning whose manifestation is sought. The breath becomes determined at one or more ranks, called externally its points of articulation. With respect to the seeking and inclination involved, speech belongs within will.</p>
<p>Power is the capacity to produce the effect through which what seeks manifestation comes to appear. For that reason it is included in speech and branches from it. Generosity consists in the demand to give preference to another, by virtue of a perfection whether belonging to essence or attribute, by giving one's person, wealth, station, or whatever is beneficial and brings perfection to anyone who deserves it, whether through actual condition or request.</p>
<p><strong>The Generous</strong> is one who possesses himself sufficiently to receive this demand and act upon it; in respect of such ability, generosity is included in power and derives from it.</p>
<p><strong>The Equitable</strong> assigns to every thing possessing a share of receptivity the share by virtue of which it may receive what the Generous bestows; hence equity belongs within generosity and comes forth from it.</p>
<p>This explains the ordering of the <strong>seven principal names</strong> in relation to each other, their successive derivation from one another in descent, and their successive inclusion within one another upon return and re-ascent.</p>
<p>The comprehensive gathering point of them all is the outward manifestation of the word <em>Allāh</em> in <strong>two respects</strong>: its existence and its reality as the determiner of its names. The reality of divinity, which is identical with the second determination and establishes what the word <em>Allāh</em> outwardly signifies, is the place where all the original and derivative realities, divine and cosmic, are gathered, arise, return, and find their point of reference. The outward aspect of the name <em>Allāh</em> therefore comprehends the names in both respects.</p>
<p>The outward aspect of <strong>al-Raḥmān</strong>, however, is their gathering point and point of return in <strong>one respect</strong>, namely existence; for <em>al-Raḥmān</em> is a name insofar as mercy is all-encompassing, and that is identical with existence.</p>
<p>The name <strong>the Living</strong> gathers them through perfection embracing all perfections; <strong>the Knowing</strong> through the universality of its relationship to known things; <strong>the Willing</strong> through seeking and inclination toward perfection.</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p38" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p38"><h3 id="title-b2007-p38">B2007 p. 38 · The names under comprehensiveness and differentiation</h3>

<p><strong>The Receptive</strong> gathers them because every one of them is a determination of the Breath of the All-merciful. <strong>The Powerful</strong> comprehends them because each is rightly said to possess a capacity to produce an effect appropriate to its own reality. <strong>The Generous</strong> gathers them because each may be said to bestow existence, as the origin of the existence of what falls within its sphere among cosmic realities and existential determinations.</p>
<p><strong>The Equitable</strong> comprehends them inasmuch as each observes the rule of the intermediate position between real unity and relational multiplicity. The universal principal names under discussion have two aspects.</p>
<p>The <strong>first</strong> is that each contains all the others, but with a hidden trace of each one's distinction through an attribute in that which manifests them, under the consideration of this mutual containment. Their containment is an effect of the unity of the comprehensive human intermediacy, in its undifferentiated form and in the exact middle of its rank. Its true comprehensiveness unites the two judgments: that of the self-disclosure, with real unity and relational multiplicity; and that of the determination, with real multiplicity and relational unity. It thus unifies the judgments of the two extremes.</p>
<p>The appearance of a hidden trace of distinction, on the other hand, is an effect of this second intermediacy's being situated within the second determination and of its powerful connection with everlastingness, one of whose most characteristic judgments is differentiation without end.</p>
<p>The <strong>second aspect</strong> of those original universal names is that they are really distinguished, and the effect proper to each becomes manifest, though a hidden trace of their mutual containment remains—in the reverse of the first aspect. Their distinction results from the differentiation of this second intermediacy, which is identical with the Cloud-like Presence. The remaining trace of mutual containment is an effect of its comprehensive character, its unity, its collective inclusion, and its precise equilibrium, which will be explained shortly, God willing.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p39" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p39"><h3 id="title-b2007-p39">B2007 p. 39 · Prophetic hierarchies and the number of the names</h3>

<p>The realities of the perfected ones who are the <strong>messengers of resolute determination</strong> (<em>ulū al-ʿazm</em>) are established and included within this comprehensive reality, appearing successively through the judgment of one of the seven original realities—in their mutual inclusion, with the hidden trace of differentiation and inclination toward descent.</p>
<p>The realities of those possessing perfection among the <strong>Muhammadan inheritors</strong> are also established and included in this comprehensive, unitary intermediacy. They manifest as the polar station (<em>quṭbiyya</em>) arising from the station of substitution (<em>badaliyya</em>) under the judgment of one of the original seven divine realities, in their mutual inclusion and with an even more concealed trace of differentiation, but now through an inclination toward re-ascent and return to their origin, identical with the Keys and first self-disclosure. The realities of the remaining seven substitutes (<em>abdāl</em>) are contained within the reality of the Pole. They arise from it and become determined within the Cloud-like Presence insofar as their differentiation predominates and their inclusion becomes concealed.</p>
<p>From these seven original divine realities arose <strong>ninety-two divine realities</strong>, completing the <strong>ninety-nine realities</strong> through which the ninety-nine names are determined. From these there arise <strong>three hundred divine realities</strong>, each inseparably connected with a divine character trait. A report states, “God possesses three hundred characteristics; whoever takes on one of them enters Paradise.” Abū Bakr asked, “Is there any of them in me, Messenger of God?” He answered, “All of them are in you.”</p>
<p>From every reality a divine name becomes determined. Within the Cloud-like Presence the realities of the messengers also arise and become determined from these divine realities. From these divine realities branch <strong>one thousand and one realities</strong>, whose names are determined by this number; and from each divine reality among them arises the reality of a human prophet within the Cloud-like Presence. From these divine realities branch the complete number of <strong>one hundred and twenty-four thousand divine realities</strong>, each corresponding to a divine name. From them arise an equal number of human prophetic realities. From the Muhammadan realities arise multiples of this number of divine realities, both principal and derivative, in this Cloud-like Presence.</p>
<p>All these are articulations of the one <strong>comprehensive Muhammadan reality</strong>, called the Reality of Realities, which permeates all things as a universal permeates its particulars. It is identical with the first, greatest, most primordial intermediacy, which is their origin. From it then branched—</p>

<p><strong>Transmission note.</strong> The parenthetic citation to the report about three hundred traits is Farghānī’s. The edition’s modern footnote compares a report about three hundred and sixty traits; its bibliographical discussion has <strong>not</strong> been inserted into the translated authorial text.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p40" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p40"><h3 id="title-b2007-p40">B2007 p. 40 · Divine lordship and the fixed entities</h3>

<p>—from these divine realities, themselves differentiated and arising from it, and from the realities attributed to all the prophets—universal principles, origins, genera from genera, and branches of branches—an almost innumerable multiplicity of derivative and particular divine realities. From them arose, in the Cloud-like Presence, at its side named the <strong>Presence of Necessity</strong> and at its other side named the <strong>Presence of Possibility</strong>, innumerable cosmic realities.</p>
<p>Whatever is related to both extremes through comprehensiveness and an analogy with their intermediate character, however slight, constitutes a <strong>human reality</strong>. Whatever has a stronger relationship to the side of necessity is a higher, simple, angelic reality; whatever has a more intense relationship to the side of possibility is a lower reality among generated things.</p>
<p>As for human realities, some incline toward the side of possibility: these are the realities of unbelievers, falling within the scope of misguidance. Others incline toward the middle and comprehensiveness or toward necessity: these are the realities of believers and saints, within the circle of the reality of guidance. The varying intensity or weakness of that inclination discloses the difference of their predispositions and degrees in receiving the light of faith and the effect of guidance.</p>
<p>All these divine and cosmic realities were essential affairs and states among the considerations of oneness, included within one another and giving rise to one another in the forms of universal and particular, original and derivative, generic and specific realities.</p>
<p>Whatever divine reality—whether its roots, branches, or branches of branches, and so on—gives rise to the determination of a thing's reality, <strong>the concrete existence of that thing</strong> through which it manifests at spiritual, imaginal and sensory ranks likewise arises from the divine name determined by that divine reality in accordance with its distinction and attribute. That name is <strong>its Lord</strong>: it receives only from Him, gives only through Him, returns only to Him in every orientation and invocation, by its condition or by speech, in every place, and witnesses only Him. We shall clarify this further shortly, God willing.</p>
<p>Those essential affairs are called <strong>realities</strong> (<em>ḥaqāʾiq</em>) here because the judgments of the second rank—where distinctions associated with everlastingness predominate, together with lingering effects of the darkness of the unseen nondelimitation and pre-eternity—surround each affair like an enclosing case (<em>ḥuqqa</em>), so that it has its own enclosure. They are called <strong>fixed entities</strong> (<em>aʿyān thābita</em>) because they remain established in the second rank and never leave it: <strong>nothing appears in concrete existence except their concomitants, judgments, and accidents</strong> insofar as these pertain to cosmic ranks.</p>
<p>They are also called <strong>quiddities</strong> (<em>māhiyyāt</em>) because inquiry asks concerning the identity or <em>thisness</em> attributed to a thing: “my soul,” “my spirit,” “my heart,” “my body,” “my whole,” or “my part.” One asks, “What is it?” (<em>mā hiya?</em>); the letter <em>hāʾ</em> of pausing is added and the consonant doubled—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p41" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p41"><h3 id="title-b2007-p41">B2007 p. 41 · The Cloud-like Presence and the limits of creaturely determination</h3>

<p>—its <em>yāʾ</em>, so that the word becomes a name for the identity and thisness in question. All these are <strong>relational matters, nonexistent in themselves</strong>, having no existence except in the knowledge of the knower who knows them.</p>
<p>It is in this <strong>Cloud-like Presence</strong> (<em>al-ḥaḍra al-ʿamāʾiyya</em>) that the Real appears with the attributes of creatures, descending [in manifestation] from the rank proper to Him, namely the Presence of Necessity. Thus things ascribed to creatures—wondering, hesitation, laughing, joyous welcome and the like—are also attributed to Him, exalted and holy. Creatures likewise appear in this Presence with attributes of their Lord, when they become freed from the bonds of multiplicity and ascend beyond the lowliest cosmic ranks, as in bringing the dead to life, healing those blind from birth and lepers, assuming the attributes of truth and transcendence, and similar instances.</p>
<p>The Prophet, peace be upon him, had this Cloud-like Presence in view when asked, “Where was our Lord before creating creation?” He replied: “He was in a cloud (<em>ʿamāʾ</em>), with no air above it and no air below it.” In Arabic, <em>ʿamāʾ</em> is a thin cloud which partly intervenes between the observer and sunlight. This intermediary, by its subtlety and fineness, stands between the reality of outward existential light and a seeing attributed to the fixed entity—a seeing that belongs to the inward existential light constituting the inward reality of every possible thing.</p>
<p>The second, outward, concrete existential self-disclosure pervades this Cloud-like Presence in the form of nurturing and setting aright. In the case of the name-related realities, this is effected by making their influences and requirements appear within cosmic realities; in the case of cosmic realities, by disclosing their proper judgments through the attribution of concrete existence to them.</p>
<p>Under its <strong>comprehensive</strong> consideration this intermediary is identical with human reality and the rank of perfection, which constitutes the measure of perfect reality and the very centre of equilibrium. Under that consideration the seven realities—the determining principles of the seven leading names—are included within it. The realities of perfected prophets and saints other than our Prophet, peace be upon him, are likewise included, appearing successively at the cosmic ranks as the concealed influence of one of these seven realities predominates in each, without excluding the rule of the other six.</p>
<p>The realities of the rest of humanity derive from these principles, their branches, and further branches. They are distinguished and articulated within the Cloud-like Presence according to their respective distances from the original principle and measure: some are nearer, others farther from <strong>perfection</strong>, and likewise from the <strong>supreme perfection</strong> peculiar to the Muhammadan reality. For the influence of this supreme and perfect intermediary pervades—</p>


</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p42" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p42"><h3 id="title-b2007-p42">B2007 p. 42 · Three classes of realities: divine, cosmic, and shared in attribution</h3>

<p>—every reality receptive to it, through which its receptivity subsists and its position between Necessity and real impossibility is maintained. From it arise genera, then species, then individuals established in all their determinations: the nearest and near in the Cloud-like Presence, the distant and more distant in the Presence of Possibility. Reflect carefully on this chapter and, God willing, you will gain the greatest treasure and the red sulphur.</p>
<p><strong>Chapter.</strong> Know that the universal ranks to be enumerated shortly, called <strong>worlds</strong> and <strong>Presences</strong>, are like the loci, scenes and places of manifestation for the other realities ascribed to the Real or to the cosmos: they encompass and contain them. These ranks themselves are <strong>intelligible realities</strong>, like the realities encompassed by them. All are impressed within the second rank as genera, principles, species, branches and individuals, and there become determined under the aspect of ranks whose names and complete enumeration will be given shortly, God willing.</p>
<p>The realities included within these ranks fall under <strong>three divisions</strong>.</p>
<p><strong>First:</strong> what is attributed exclusively to the Real. Examples are divinity, the essential mercy embracing all things—which is existence considered under the aspect of overflowing bestowal—essential necessity, self-subsistence (<em>qayyūmiyya</em>), meaning subsisting in itself and making another subsist, essential self-sufficiency, and other such realities.</p>
<p><strong>Second:</strong> what is attributed to the cosmos, such as poverty, essential nonexistence, abjection, possibility, and multiplicity. These are all dependent realities following principal realities: for example, the reality of spirit, angel, celestial sphere, elements, heaven and earth, and generated beings.</p>
<p><strong>Third:</strong> what is attributed originally to the Real but to the cosmos secondarily through the attribution of existence to it, such as knowledge, will, and similar attributes. They may be ascribed to the Real and are then eternal, or to the cosmos and are then temporally originated.</p>
<p>Among these realities, some are <strong>universal</strong>, such as human reality and knowledge; others are <strong>particular</strong>, such as the reality of Zayd and Zayd's knowledge. Among particulars, some are principal, such as the reality of Zayd, while others are concomitants, attributes, properties and accidents belonging to that principal reality: its life, speech, receptivity, possibility, knowledge, ignorance, its intelligible, spiritual, imaginal or sensory configuration, its outward manifestation and hiddenness, the attribution of existence to it, and the like.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p43" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p43"><h3 id="title-b2007-p43">B2007 p. 43 · The five universal ranks and the sixth comprehensive rank</h3>

<p>As for the universal and principal realities, they remain restricted to the beginning of the Presence of Knowledge and the second rank. Their concomitants, attributes, properties and accidents, however, are established throughout its middle and end. Some accompany them in that Presence of Knowledge itself, such as their original unmade receptivity and intelligible configuration. Others fall within the world of spirits: their life and knowledge, their spiritual configuration, their outward appearance in the spiritual world as included within their genus and species or distinguished as individuals there, and their hiddenness with respect to the imaginal and sensory worlds—as also the attribution of existence to them within the spiritual world.</p>
<p>Other concomitants fall within the imaginal world: their imaginal configuration, their manifestation there, and knowledge ascribed to such a configuration, and the like. Still others fall within the sensory world: their sensible configuration, their appearance there, and the attribution of existence to them in it; their existential receptivity for the sciences and actions; and their possession of the <strong>ten categories</strong>, such as quality, quantity and so on.</p>
<p>These universal ranks are restricted to <strong>five</strong>: two attributed to the Real and three attributed to the cosmos; a <strong>sixth</strong> comprehends them all. For these ranks are loci and sites of self-disclosure. Any such rank is either a locus in which things appear <strong>to the Real alone</strong>, and not to cosmic things, or a locus in which things appear to the Real <strong>and</strong> to cosmic things.</p>
<p>The first kind is called the <strong>rank of the Unseen</strong>, because every cosmic thing is concealed there from itself and from its like; nothing appears within it except to the Real. Such non-appearance of things has two forms.</p>
<p>The <strong>first</strong> is the complete negation of their entities: “God was and there was nothing with Him.” Their manifestation in knowledge and finding is therefore absent insofar as their entities are entirely absent. This locus is the <strong>first determination</strong> and the <strong>first rank of the Unseen</strong>.</p>
<p>The <strong>second</strong> consists in the nonexistence of the attribute of outward appearance for things, even though their entities are realized, differentiated and established in eternal knowledge and apparent to the Knower—but <strong>not apparent to themselves or to their likes</strong>. This resembles forms established within our own minds. This locus is the <strong>second determination</strong>, the <strong>world of meanings</strong>, and the <strong>second rank</strong>; it too is called Unseen for the reason given.</p>
<p>As for a locus in which cosmic things also find what appears to them through knowledge and finding, it has <strong>three divisions</strong>. Such a locus can be one in which things appear to cosmic entities—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p44" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p44"><h3 id="title-b2007-p44">B2007 p. 44 · Spirit, imagination, and sense; names are not their words</h3>

<p>—whose existences are simple in themselves. That is called the <strong>rank of spirits</strong>. Or it may be the locus in which things appear to compound existents. These compound existents may be so <strong>subtle</strong> that they do not admit division, partial separation, rupture or rejoining; the locus of their appearance, and of the things appearing to them, is called the <strong>imaginal rank</strong> (<em>martabat al-mithāl</em>).</p>
<p>Alternatively, the compound existents may be <strong>dense</strong>, in comparison with such subtleties or actually in themselves, so that they admit division, separation, rupture and rejoining. Their locus, the locus of their attribute of outward manifestation, and that in which things appear to them is called the <strong>sensory rank</strong>, the <strong>world of witnessing</strong>, and the <strong>world of bodies</strong>. The true Perfect Human and the one most perfect comprehends all these by virtue of manifesting the second and first intermediary ranks. Thus, by God's aid, the universal ranks have been comprehensively enumerated.</p>
<p><strong>Chapter.</strong> Know that the realities of the divine names subsisting in the holy Essence, transcendent of alteration and change, are <strong>not identical with spoken expressions</strong> formed from separate letters which change, are substituted, and vary according to language, construction and pronunciation. The expressions are <strong>names of those names</strong>, signs indicating their meanings; the realities subsisting in the Essence are what the expressions mean and designate.</p>
<p>For the reality of the name <em>Allāh</em> is the Essence's self-disclosure and determination as the <strong>One comprehending all self-disclosures and determinations</strong>, subsisting in the Essence. The Arabic word <em>Allāh</em> has the meaning of Persian <em>Khodāy</em> and Turkish <em>Tengri</em>, while the words vary, change and alternate. The reality to which they point transcends such variation; consequently they are names of the names, <strong>not the realities themselves</strong>.</p>
<p>Once this is understood, we say that the divine names are, in reality, of <strong>two kinds</strong>, negative and affirmative. All fall under <strong>three universal degrees</strong>: first, names of the Essence; second, names of the attributes; third, names of the acts.</p>
<p>The ground of this classification is that the <strong>name in reality is the Essence</strong>—or say, existence—but <strong>not under its nondelimitation</strong>; rather, under some consideration and determination. If the consideration and determination are identical with the Essence, as with the first determination, true unity, absolute self-sufficiency, preceding and prevailing essential mercy, and the like, the Essence under that determination is <strong>one of the names of the Essence</strong>. Such are the realities of <em>Allāh</em>, <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, <em>al-Raḥīm</em>, the One Self-sufficient of all worlds, the Keys of the Unseen, and the essentially One and One-in-Unicity. If the consideration and determination are not—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p45" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p45"><h3 id="title-b2007-p45">B2007 p. 45 · Negative and affirmative names; levels of divine disclosure</h3>

<p>—identical [with the Essence in that way], and no effect extends from that determination to another in any of the cosmic ranks, it is a <strong>name of an attribute</strong>, such as the Knowing and the Willing. If an effect extends from it to another in the rank of spirits, imaginal forms or sense, it is a <strong>name of an act</strong>, such as the Creator, the Originator and the Fashioner.</p>
<p>Moreover, if the determination or consideration signifies the <strong>negation</strong> of a consideration from the Essence, as do the concepts of unicity, everlastingness, pre-eternity, and the like, the name under that aspect is <strong>negative</strong>, such as the One-in-Unicity and the Unique. If it signifies the <strong>affirmation</strong> of some consideration, as with oneness, eternal mercy and the like, the name under that aspect is <strong>affirmative</strong>, such as the One and the names <em>Allāh</em>, <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, and <em>al-Raḥīm</em> attributed to the Essence in “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful,” and as attributes in “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, the Compassionate, the Merciful” (Qurʾān 1:2–3).</p>
<p>The locus of disclosure of the <strong>realities of the essential names</strong> is therefore the first rank and the precise centre of the second rank: the human intermediary, containing the seven original realities and leading names, each of which comprehends all the others, though a hidden trace particular to each appears within it.</p>
<p>The locus of disclosure of the <strong>names of attributes</strong> is the Cloud-like Presence, the aspect in which this human intermediary becomes differentiated, and the place where the distinctions of the seven principles and their particular effects become manifest.</p>
<p>The loci of disclosure of the <strong>names of acts</strong> are all the cosmic ranks, insofar as these are impressed within the second rank, since the complete display of the effects of the divine acts depends on them.</p>
<p>Consequently, God's disclosure to His servants <strong>through the acts</strong> occurs only within cosmic manifestations—spiritual, imaginal or sensory. His disclosure <strong>through the attributes</strong> occurs only when one is stripped of all the judgments and manifestations of cosmic ranks. A flash of His <strong>essential self-disclosure</strong> occurs only through solitude from all the judgments of multiplicity and the realities of distinctions among names and attributes.</p>
<p>There may remain, however, a hidden trace manifested precisely in the centre of the second human intermediacy, while the judgment of unification and inclusion predominates. Such isolation is attained through <strong>true annihilation after annihilation</strong> (<em>al-fanāʾ al-ḥaqīqī baʿd al-fanāʾ</em>).</p>
<p>The attributive realities determining the names are initially divided into <strong>relative</strong> ones, such as manifestation, hiddenness, firstness and lastness; and <strong>nonrelative</strong> ones, such as knowledge, will, and their fundamental and derivative attributes. The nonrelative realities divide again into two kinds: one having no opposite of its own kind with a contrary effect and property, as with will and power; the other having a counterpart and opposite, as with guidance and leading astray and their concomitants, or satisfaction and anger. Both opposed attributes arise from branches of—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p46" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p46"><h3 id="title-b2007-p46">B2007 p. 46 · Eight classes of names; manifest and concealed names</h3>

<p>—the <strong>unopposed</strong> [attributes]. Among opposed attributes some signify change of state, such as contraction and expansion, and the names determined from them are called <strong>names of states</strong>.</p>
<p>The <strong>names of acts</strong> fall into two categories. One comprises acts mentioned in revelation <strong>without a corresponding name</strong>, such as “God subjected,” “God became angry,” “God cursed,” and “God leads astray,” and similar expressions. The other comprises those of which both <strong>the act and its name</strong> occur, such as “God creates whatever He wills” and “God is Creator of every thing.” These make <strong>eight categories</strong> into which all the divine names are distributed, corresponding to the original gates of Paradise. Understand this.</p>
<p>The name-related realities themselves belong to two kinds. Some have <strong>no outward expression</strong> indicating them as their name in any language, or in some languages. This is intended in the supplication: “O God, I ask You by every name belonging to You, by which You have named Yourself, or which You have sent down in Your Book, or taught to one of Your creatures, or reserved for Yourself within Your knowledge of the Unseen.” In one sense the Keys of the Unseen belong among these.</p>
<p>The second kind has an outward form expressed <strong>in words or in writing</strong> through which we recognize the name. That kind is subdivided into two: first, <strong>pronouns</strong>, such as “He,” “I,” “we,” the second-person <em>kāf</em>, the second-person <em>tāʾ</em>, and pronouns of third person and plural; and second, <strong>explicit nominal expressions</strong>, such as <em>Allāh</em>, the Knowing, the Creator, and their likes.</p>
<p>All pronouns designate <strong>realities of the essential names</strong>, but under differing considerations. The third-person pronoun indicates the Essence insofar as the judgment of hiddenness predominates over that of presence. The second-person pronoun indicates the reverse. The plural pronoun indicates the attachment of one or more names to the self-disclosure, while a singular pronoun indicates the self-disclosure alone, or a single name alone.</p>
<p>The explicit expressions include <strong>all three classes</strong> of names: essential, attributive and act-related. All the names described here are <strong>established through authoritative disclosure</strong> (<em>tawqīfī</em>) according to the correct view; they are known only through revelation, genuine unveiling, or explicit divine communication.</p>
<p>After the essential names established at the first rank—such as the inward realities of the names <em>Allāh</em>, <em>al-Raḥmān</em> and <em>al-Raḥīm</em>, the essential One and One-in-Unicity—the principles of the divine names are the <strong>seven leading names</strong>. The first, most comprehensive, and most perfect of them is <strong>the Living</strong>, insofar as it is itself—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p47" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p47"><h3 id="title-b2007-p47">B2007 p. 47 · Three modes of enumerating and realizing the ninety-nine names</h3>

<p>—perfection and its source, with awareness of the entirety and comprehensive character of that perfection. From these original, leading names branch the remainder needed to complete the number of the <strong>ninety-nine names</strong>. Anyone who enumerates them through <strong>relation</strong> (<em>taʿalluq</em>), <strong>adoption of their qualities</strong> (<em>takhalluq</em>), or <strong>realization</strong> (<em>taḥaqquq</em>) enters Paradise.</p>
<p>Their enumeration by <strong>relation</strong> consists in seeking the effects of each name within one's own soul and body, every faculty, member and part, throughout the totality of one's states and spiritual and corporeal configurations, and through all one's transformations and varied manifestations: sleeping and waking; standing and sitting; obedience and disobedience; contraction and expansion; health and illness; contentment and anger; pleasure and pain; ease and hardship; spaciousness and constriction; wealth and poverty, and so on.</p>
<p>One sees all these as judgments belonging to the divine names, attributing whatever becomes manifest within oneself to those names and their effects. Then one responds to each as appropriate: with gratitude or patience, humble entreaty or excuse, self-abasement or submission, modesty, humbling oneself, recourse and seeking refuge, brokenness, regret, seeking forgiveness, asking for help or guidance, and other descriptions of servanthood, thereby discharging the obligation of the rights of Lordship.</p>
<p>By such enumeration and reckoning, and performance of the due right according to one's greatest capacity and effort, one enters the <strong>Garden of Works</strong>. It is the place where transient and perishing accidents—of speech, action, intention, and belief—are concealed beneath the forms of abiding, fixed entities: heavenly companions, palaces, attendants and gardens.</p>
<p>Enumeration through <strong>adoption of the names' qualities</strong> takes place when the spiritual spirit aspires toward the realities, meanings, and attributes of these names, assuming and being characterized by the reality of each in conformity with the injunction “Take on the character traits of God.” Through this enumeration, followed by such assumption and characterization, one enters the <strong>Garden of Inheritance</strong>, which is higher than the first Garden, or rather its inward aspect, inclined toward the <em>malakūt</em> side. It is hidden in the spiritual sovereignty of every thing as it descends into the form of nature, but under the aspect that adjoins the world of spirits, not the sensory world where the Garden of Works appears.</p>
<p>The Prophet, peace be upon him, is cited as saying: “There is none among you but that he has a dwelling in the Garden and a dwelling in the Fire. When an unbeliever dies and enters the Fire, the people of the Garden inherit his dwelling. If you wish, recite: ‘Those are the inheritors, who—’”</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p48" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p48"><h3 id="title-b2007-p48">B2007 p. 48 · Realization and the Garden of Grace</h3>

<p>“—inherit Paradise, in which they shall dwell forever” (Qurʾān 23:10–11). These dwellings arise through the orientation of the <em>malakūt</em> toward descent for the manifestation of the worlds of nature and sense.</p>
<p>As for enumeration through <strong>realization</strong> (<em>taḥaqquq</em>), this occurs through Godwariness (<em>taqwā</em>) and divesting oneself of every form, meaning and effect subsisting within one and appearing through one that is marked by origination, and through being concealed within the clouds of their entities, secrets and lights. One then enters the <strong>Garden of Gracious Bestowal</strong> (<em>jannat al-imtinān</em>), the station of concealment within the unseen of the Unseen, alluded to by the words: “Indeed the Godwary are in a secure station, amid gardens and springs” (Qurʾān 44:51–52), prepared with what no eye has seen, no ear heard, and what has not occurred to any human heart.</p>
<p>Let us now return to our subject: identifying how each group of the remaining branches that complete the ninety-nine names belongs to its original principle among the names included in this number.</p>
<p>We say that <strong>the Living</strong>—identical with perfection and its source, apprehending perfection in its universal, comprehensive character—contains and includes every name associated with any perfection, as indicated before. Some perfections concern inwardness; others concern outwardness.</p>
<p>Among the inward perfections is <strong>the Magnificent</strong> (<em>al-ʿAẓīm</em>), whose affair fills the cosmos but whose ultimate nature is concealed from creatures, preventing their limited and lowly intellects, imaginations and understandings from grasping the perfection of His affair and the majesty of His rank.</p>
<p>There is also <strong>the Great</strong> (<em>al-Kabīr</em>): because the perfection of His rank is remote from attainment, creatures recognize their smallness and innately testify that He is greater than anything which appears great.</p>
<p>There is <strong>the Exalted</strong> (<em>al-ʿAlī</em>), whose perfect exaltedness surpasses every means of apprehension; <strong>the Majestic</strong> (<em>al-Jalīl</em>), whose majestic unicity transcends the attribution of anything to Him; <strong>the Self-sufficient</strong> (<em>al-Ghanī</em>), independent of all worlds by the perfection of His sufficiency in the unseen of His Unseen, contemplating the beauty of His majesty and His considerations within the first determination of His most holy Essence; and <strong>the All-holy</strong> (<em>al-Quddūs</em>), perfectly exempt from blameworthy attributes and from attribution to Him of deficiencies of acts and effects, and the like.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p49" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p49"><h3 id="title-b2007-p49">B2007 p. 49 · The Living, the All-comprehending, and the Self-subsisting</h3>

<p>With respect to <strong>outward</strong> perfection, all affirmative names are branches of the Living insofar as they involve some perfection. The greatness of His affair becomes apparent through what He brings forth in the cosmos, so that creatures recognize both the smallness of their own measures and His superiority over them. All share in createdness, and their determinate share of existence, judgment and effect is limited: no creature can go beyond the share assigned to it. Thus smallness belongs to them, and none has a right to be great or to boast of greatness. Hence arises the judgment of the name <strong>the Supremely Great</strong> (<em>al-Mutakabbir</em>), which belongs to Him alone.</p>
<p>Because He embraces outwardly and inwardly all the names and realities pertaining to every perfection, there arises from Him <strong>the Gatherer</strong> (<em>al-Jāmiʿ</em>). Because hidden perfections, diffused from Him and inwardly present in names and realities, are concealed from the cosmos, there arises <strong>the Inward</strong> (<em>al-Bāṭin</em>). Because He is the principle from which the details and distinctions of the names arise, there arises <strong>the First</strong> (<em>al-Awwal</em>). Because all praises and celebrations of perfection, supremacy, and glory ultimately come to Him, there arise <strong>the Praiseworthy</strong> (<em>al-Ḥamīd</em>) and <strong>the Glorious</strong> (<em>al-Majīd</em>).</p>
<p>Because every negative name arises from Him, the <strong>forms</strong> of the names the One and One-in-Unicity arise—not their ultimate realities, for those realities belong to the essential names at the first rank. Thus the Living is the source of all the principles, as we have explained. Even the outward aspect of <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, in that His bestowal extends generally to created beings, and of <em>al-Raḥīm</em>, insofar as His bestowal is specifically related to the rightly guided, are comprehended collectively within the Living.</p>
<p>Yet from the standpoint of <strong>the nondelimitation of existential mercy</strong> and the all-bestowing power of the name <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, the Living itself, with every name it contains, is among its branches.</p>
<p>Two names are especially closely associated with the Living: one insofar as He is perfection itself and its source; another insofar as He apprehends perfection as a complete whole. The first is <strong>the Self-subsisting</strong> (<em>al-Qayyūm</em>), meaning that He subsists through Himself and every thing subsists through Him. His inseparability from the Living is so strong that His name is mentioned only together with and within it. Some realized investigators therefore regard <strong>the Living, the Self-subsisting</strong> (<em>al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm</em>) as one compound name, like a compound proper name, just as some have said of “the One, the One-in-Unicity.”</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p50" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p50"><h3 id="title-b2007-p50">B2007 p. 50 · Subsistence, abiding, truth, and delegated care</h3>

<p>The other of the two names is <strong>the Governor</strong> (<em>al-Mudabbir</em>), who witnesses the whole and totality of every affair on which its particular parts and details depend.</p>
<p>From <strong>the Self-subsisting</strong> arises <strong>the Abiding</strong> (<em>al-Bāqī</em>), who remains established and enduring when destruction and annihilation overtake the descriptions, accidents, determinations and relationships that become attached to the very reality of His existence. All these perish and disappear, while the very reality of His existence remains. It had faced the realities of possible things, and through that confrontation those accidents and relations were attached to it. What had no beginningless reality perishes, and what never ceased to be remains—namely His Face confronting generated things, as explained already. God says, “Do not invoke another deity beside God: there is no deity but Him. Every thing perishes except His Face. His is the judgment, and to Him you return” (Qurʾān 28:88), and “All upon it shall perish; the Face of your Lord, possessed of majesty and honor, remains” (Qurʾān 55:26–27). Hence arises the name <strong>the Last</strong> (<em>al-Ākhir</em>).</p>
<p>From the Abiding also arises <strong>the Real</strong> (<em>al-Ḥaqq</em>), the one of two things that remains established. Strictly speaking it is a name of existence, which confronts possible reality—that is, nonexistence—with its receptivity and preparedness. Nonexistence vanishes, while what confronts it remains: everlasting, abiding existence. For this reason existence itself, considered as its universal outspread overflowing, is called <strong>the Real through which every thing is created</strong>, as in “We created the heavens, the earth, and what is between them only through truth” (Qurʾān 15:85).</p>
<p>From the name Abiding comes <strong>the Inheritor</strong> (<em>al-Wārith</em>), to whom all possessions and disposals ultimately return as independent sovereignty when those to whom they were attributed have perished, in accordance with “Everything perishes except His Face.”</p>
<p>From the Self-subsisting and the Abiding also arise <strong>the Giver of life</strong> and <strong>the Preserver in being</strong>. Among the names dependent on the Living is <strong>the Ever-besought</strong> (<em>al-Ṣamad</em>), to whom needs are directed and in whom sovereignty culminates, to whom people turn for the fulfillment of wants, for He is fully able to supply them and needs no other.</p>
<p>Since the Self-subsisting subsists through Himself and makes all else subsist, He independently undertakes every affair. If a servant entrusts his affairs to Him, He undertakes them on the servant's behalf, condescending through mercy and kindness, as He had undertaken them independently. At that point He receives the name <strong>the Trustee</strong> (<em>al-Wakīl</em>), a branch of the Self-subsisting.</p>
<p>Know next that the reality of life is the form of the first receptivity: identical with knowledge of the most holy Essence, the first determination, and original love. The manifestation of that original love—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p51" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p51"><h3 id="title-b2007-p51">B2007 p. 51 · Divine will as the Throne of disclosure</h3>

<p>—in the second determination is the reality of <strong>divine will</strong> (<em>mashīʾa</em>), which gives all realities the name “thing” and the reality of thinghood. Just as the second determination manifests the first, and life manifests the first receptivity, so divine will is one of the attributes most properly inseparable from life, which is receptivity to every perfection.</p>
<p>The name Living comprehends all names universally and collectively; will, however, assigns to each its specific judgment and perfection and orders all of them, making one prior or posterior to another in nobility, rank, universality or particularity, originality or derivation.
