Knowledge comprises the things known, while will orders them and assigns some precedence in rank and existence.</p>
<p>Since will is among the most proper concomitants of life, which is—as we have said—receptivity to every appropriate perfection, <strong>the outward, all-merciful existential self-disclosure</strong>, as the source of every perfection and its manifestation in receptive loci according to their capacities, is disclosed only within will. Hence <strong>will is its Throne</strong>.</p>
<p>Shaykh Abū Ṭālib, perceiving that will must universally accompany the locus of disclosure—since it discloses to whomsoever it wishes, wherever and in whatever locus it wishes, or without a locus if it wishes—said: “Its Throne is His will.” Divine will subsists through holy knowledge related to the most holy Essence; it is a form of one of the considerations of oneness, identical with knowledge there. Knowledge, inasmuch as its benefit is universal and its effects all-pervading, is frequently figured by <strong>water</strong> because of their close correspondence.</p>
<p>Do you not see how Ibn ʿAbbās interpreted “He sent down water from the sky, and the valleys flowed according to their capacities” (Qurʾān 13:17), saying: “The water is knowledge and the valleys are hearts”? Thus the Qurʾān says, “His Throne was upon the water” (11:7). His Throne is His will, whose subsistence and realization are in essential knowledge identical with the Essence. Will is a relation with no establishment or actuality except through, from, and within this knowledge. Know this; God is the Guide.</p>
<p>After the Living among the seven original names comes <strong>the Knowing</strong> (<em>al-ʿAlīm</em>). Everything that the Living apprehended collectively and universally, the Governor ordered, and divine will made into distinct things among the considerations of oneness and assigned particular judgments and meanings, appears to the Knowing as articulated and distinct.</p>
<p>If what appears to knowledge is the Essence itself through forms of the considerations of oneness, without describing these forms as others, the Knowing is called <strong>the Outward</strong> (<em>al-Ẓāhir</em>). If the forms that appear are not qualified as self-identical or other, and their relationship to inwardness is stronger while they appear without intermediary, there arises from the Knowing <strong>the Aware</strong> (<em>al-Khabīr</em>). If their relation to outwardness is stronger and they possess an intelligible or formal configuration appearing to the Knowing through a light issuing from Him and connected to them, there arises from Him the name—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p52" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p52"><h3 id="title-b2007-p52">B2007 p. 52 · Fourteen names branching from the Knowing</h3>

<p>—<strong>the Seeing</strong> (<em>al-Baṣīr</em>). If what appears to the Knowing has a relation to manifestation, namely breath, and a relation to inwardness, namely the meaning contained within that breath, and a relation of turning toward receptivity for this meaning through something joining them, called speech, there arises <strong>the Hearing</strong> (<em>al-Samīʿ</em>).</p>
<p>The Hearing and Seeing, when considered as arising from knowledge insofar as knowledge is identical with the Essence at the first rank, are <strong>essential names and Keys of the Unseen</strong>; when considered as arising from the Knowing at the second rank, they are <strong>names of attributes</strong>. Likewise, the One and One-in-Unicity, when their realization is considered at the first rank, are essential names; otherwise, they are attributive names branching from the Living, as explained earlier. The same applies to the Speaking and the Strong. Keep this well in mind, for it is extremely useful.</p>
<p>Insofar as the Knowing encompasses everything appearing to Him, so that His capacity embraces everything without one thing crowding out another, there arise <strong>the Encompassing</strong> (<em>al-Muḥīṭ</em>) and <strong>the Vast</strong> (<em>al-Wāsiʿ</em>). When one considers the Knowing's presence alongside what appears to Him, without any possibility of its absence from Him, and the disclosure of another that verifies what is manifest to Him, there is determined in one sense <strong>the Witness</strong> (<em>al-Shahīd</em>).</p>
<p>From His encompassing what is outward and inward in what appears to Him, and what belongs to it, so completely that He cannot lose it, there arises <strong>the Finder</strong> (<em>al-Wājid</em>). From the appearance to Him of the inward aspect of everything through its all-pervading character, there arises <strong>the Subtle</strong> (<em>al-Laṭīf</em>). From the Knowing's unveiling of that which should remain hidden from others among the inner judgments of what appears to Him, there arises <strong>the Light</strong> (<em>al-Nūr</em>).</p>
<p>From the full manifestation to Him of every thing, and of its defects, together with the care to safeguard it against those defects, arises <strong>the Watchful</strong> (<em>al-Raqīb</em>). By securing the foundation on which what appears to Him becomes manifest, strengthening its manifestation, there branches <strong>the Wise</strong> (<em>al-Ḥakīm</em>). From the appearance to Him of a thing and what opposes it, while the consequences and predominance of the opposing thing are warded off, arises <strong>the Preserver</strong> (<em>al-Ḥafīẓ</em>).</p>
<p>Inasmuch as what appears to the Knowing is manifest to Him outwardly and inwardly, so that no hidden aspect of a thing's identity nor any outward sign remains concealed, and His witnessing and testimony are complete knowledge, there arises <strong>the Guardian-Witness</strong> (<em>al-Muhaymin</em>). Inasmuch as the appearance of what is known gives it security against hiddenness and ignorance and the injuries they bring, there arises <strong>the Giver of Security</strong> (<em>al-Muʾmin</em>).</p>
<p>These are <strong>fourteen names</strong> whose relationship and derivation belong specifically to the Knowing, while the other names can also participate in derivation from this and the other principles.</p>
<p>As for <strong>the Willing</strong>, it seeks and inclines toward specifying a thing through existence or nonexistence, through precedence or posteriority, or any meaning and judgment, while what is sought is manifest to it in all the requirements of its reality, such as receptivity, preparedness, beginning and end—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p53" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p53"><h3 id="title-b2007-p53">B2007 p. 53 · Guidance, misguidance, awakening, nearness, and determination</h3>

<p>Insofar as the Willing inclines to manifest the mark of knowledge amid the darkness of hiddenness, the judgments of possibility or the multiplicity of nature, there arises <strong>the Guide</strong> (<em>al-Hādī</em>). That mark of knowledge may be the original disposition upon which human beings are formed, through receptivity; or the discerning intellect that distinguishes the good and evil of an ultimate outcome, perfected by knowledge of revealed law which discloses the ends of matters and their benefit or harm. Such knowledge brings those traveling the path of triumph and salvation to the origin of light and unity.</p>
<p>Insofar as the Willing inclines to conceal these markers, because the judgments of possibility and natural multiplicity or hidden darkness predominate over certain entities, and because their essential receptivity to the manifestation of knowledge is weak, the straight road of return to the origin of light becomes obscure to them. Hence arises <strong>the One Who Leads Astray</strong> (<em>al-Muḍill</em>).</p>
<p>From the inclination to bring near the paths of seekers traveling toward Him, in accordance with “To Him the whole affair returns” (Qurʾān 11:123), arises <strong>the Rightly Directing</strong> (<em>al-Rashīd</em>).</p>
<p>From the inclination to stir something lying still in a state, quality, or condition—such as sleep, death, or any other—and move it toward a different state or quality, such as waking or life, arises <strong>the Raiser</strong> (<em>al-Bāʿith</em>).</p>
<p>From the inclination to bring a thing to perfection by removing impediments and disagreeable matters from it, with an established inclination that does not change when a contrary attribute or judgment appears from it, arises <strong>the Loving</strong> (<em>al-Wadūd</em>).</p>
<p>From the inclination to remove intermediaries between one Presence among His comprehensive Presences and a thing, bringing the thing so near that it is immediately next to Him without intermediary, and ultimately showing that nearness to it, arises <strong>the Friend or Protector</strong> (<em>al-Walī</em>), in respect of the Real—and also for the thing which receives that witnessing from Him.</p>
<p>From the inclination to cause matters to occur contrary to the sequence suggested by the outward wisdom connected with causes—bringing forward or postponing an event beyond the time in which it would occur when outward causes alone are considered—arise <strong>the One Who Brings Forward</strong> and <strong>the One Who Postpones</strong> (<em>al-Muqaddim</em>, <em>al-Muʾakhkhir</em>). Among their judgments is “I do not know what will be done with me or with you” (Qurʾān 46:9).</p>
<p>From the inclination to assign the known measure of each thing—its ordering, configuration, time, quality and quantity—so that knowledge relates to it only under that determination, arises <strong>the Determiner</strong> (<em>al-Muqaddir</em>).</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p54" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p54"><h3 id="title-b2007-p54">B2007 p. 54 · Restraint, harm, abasement, elevation, and acceptance</h3>

<p>Strictly speaking, the name <strong>the Determiner</strong> arises from divine will (<em>mashīʾa</em>), from which intention or willing (<em>irāda</em>) itself arises, and so belongs among the names dependent on the Living.</p>
<p>Insofar as the Willing inclines to repel what opposes the realization of a thing—its contrary, rival, or opponent, whether in substance, attribute, state, or otherwise—and prevent the consequences of opposition from appearing between them, there arises <strong>the Preventer</strong> (<em>al-Māniʿ</em>). From the inclination to disclose the effect of that opposition and make one of the opponents predominate over the other arises <strong>the One Who Causes Harm</strong> (<em>al-Ḍārr</em>). This judgment is most conspicuous in the contrast between guidance and leading astray.</p>
<p>From the inclination to assign to certain things a lowering of honor, rank, wealth, eminence, condition or means of living, in this world or the next or both, and to others an elevation in these respects, arise <strong>the Abaser</strong> and <strong>the Exalter</strong> (<em>al-Khāfiḍ</em>, <em>al-Rāfiʿ</em>). The Determiner may also participate in bringing these names forth.</p>
<p>From the inclination to seize and retain the totality of that by which something is sustained and prevent it from freely dispersing—for example, retaining the water and air sustaining a tree instead of letting them diffuse through its parts; holding back the breath instead of releasing it; restraining the soul from diffusing through its outward faculties and from indulging its appetites; or holding the totality of one's wealth back from meeting needs through miserliness—there arises <strong>the Withholder or Constrictor</strong> (<em>al-Qābiḍ</em>).</p>
<p>By the contrary inclination to furnish whatever sustains a thing, releasing and spreading it throughout the corresponding cases, there arises <strong>the Expander</strong> (<em>al-Bāsiṭ</em>).</p>
<p>From the inclination to single out a thing for a judgment based on the appearance of some goodness under a <strong>specified aspect</strong>, not goodness unqualifiedly, that goodness being a perfection of the thing under that aspect, arise <strong>choosing</strong> and the name <strong>the Chooser</strong> (<em>al-Mukhtār</em>). Although the name does not occur in revelation, the act and its effect do.</p>
<p>From the inclination toward something under a judgment whose conformity to the object, or to an existent or quasi-existent judgment, is agreeable according to revelation or nature, arises <strong>contentment</strong> (<em>riḍā</em>). In relation to the Real, this belongs under the Guide.</p>
<p>From the inclination to exact recompense for a judgment appearing in one thing through a judgment appearing in another, arises the reality of <strong>anger</strong> (<em>ghaḍab</em>), though revelation does not supply a separate name derived from it. It is among the results of the judgments of—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p55" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p55"><h3 id="title-b2007-p55">B2007 p. 55 · The Avenger, the Praiseworthy, the Thankful, and the Reckoner</h3>

<p>—<strong>the One Who Leads Astray</strong>, whose manifestation is opposed by the judgments of <strong>the Guide</strong>, so that the Willing brings forth an inclination to retaliate, for the sake of the Guide, against what the judgments of the One Who Leads Astray have produced in the one who receives them. This occurs only after excuses have been exhausted and proof established.</p>
<p>From the inclination to take people to account after excuses have been exhausted, using the strongest overpowering force the servant can imagine among punishments, and thereby exacting satisfaction for some judgments of the names from others, arises <strong>the Avenger</strong> (<em>al-Muntaqim</em>). These names all depend on the Willing.</p>
<p>As for <strong>the Speaking</strong> (<em>al-Qāʾil</em>): insofar as He mentions Himself and all the outward and inward perfections belonging to Him, without any deficiency or blame whatsoever, there arises <strong>the Praiseworthy</strong> (<em>al-Ḥamīd</em>) in the sense of <em>the One Who Praises</em>. In the sense of <em>the One Praised</em>, however, this name branches from the Living, as stated before.</p>
<p>Insofar as He mentions Himself and others, and what extends from Himself to the loci of manifestation of His perfections through favor and beneficence, and those loci receive the capacity to perform the duties owed for them, there arises <strong>the Thankful</strong> (<em>al-Shakūr</em>). In reality He thanks none but Himself, in accordance with “Whatever blessing you possess is from God” (Qurʾān 16:53): every blessing, including acceptance and being granted success, falls under this. Thus He is both the One Who Thanks and the One Who Is Thanked.</p>
<p>Insofar as He answers those who ask and responds to their invocations—when they say “My Lord!” answering “At your service, My servant!” as reported—and fulfills their aims sooner or later, inevitably, there arises <strong>the Responsive</strong> (<em>al-Mujīb</em>).</p>
<p>Insofar as the Speaking completes the enumeration of numbered things, up to a limit or without limit, in order to deliver various forms of sustaining aid to every one of them in creation and preservation, and to give each, noble or humble, what is due according to its entitlement, there arises <strong>the Enumerator</strong> (<em>al-Muḥṣī</em>). Enumeration without limit belongs to Him alone, exalted and holy, while limited enumeration is shared by some creatures in certain respects.</p>
<p>Insofar as He counts every numbered being and describes it minutely and comprehensively so as to supply its due sufficiency and requite its acts appropriately in this world or the next, there arises <strong>the Reckoner</strong> (<em>al-Ḥasīb</em>). Considered differently, the Reckoner may be a branch of the Living, if derived from <em>ḥasab</em>—honor and eminence—which involves a perfection sustained by the Living.</p>
<p>Insofar as He reports and testifies with perfect knowledge of Himself, saying, “God bears witness that there is no deity but He,” and testifies concerning His angels that they do not disobey Him and do what—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p56" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p56"><h3 id="title-b2007-p56">B2007 p. 56 · The Witness, the Creator, and the difference between power and strength</h3>

<p>—they are commanded to do; and concerning His books that they are light and guidance; and concerning His messengers that they acknowledged the covenant taken from them, whereupon He said, “Bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses” (Qurʾān 3:81); and concerning believers, “Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God: some have fulfilled their vow and others await, without changing their commitment” (Qurʾān 33:23)—some fulfilled their commitment in this life, discharged what they owed and attained their aim; others await its completion in the hereafter, yet none has altered the covenant. In respect of this reporting and testimony there arises from the Speaking <strong>the Witness</strong> (<em>al-Shahīd</em>).</p>
<p>The origin of <strong>bringing into existence</strong> belongs to the Speaking, in accordance with “Our word to a thing when We will it is only to say to it ‘Be!’ and it is” (Qurʾān 16:40). The Powerful contributes to it only the sustaining efficacy of bringing the effect about. Accordingly, insofar as <strong>the Creator</strong> (<em>al-Khāliq</em>) signifies the One Who Causes Existence, it is more appropriate to assign it as a branch of the Speaking.</p>
<p>The Arabic word <em>khalq</em> has three meanings. First, <strong>measuring or determining</strong>, as when one says “I fashioned the sandal” in the sense of cutting it to a pattern. Second, <strong>bringing together</strong>, whence <em>khalīqa</em> for the aggregate of created beings. Third, <strong>cutting</strong>, as in “I fashioned this according to that,” meaning cutting it to a specified measure.</p>
<p>In the first sense, the Creator belongs among the names dependent on divine will, which falls within the Living. In the second, the meaning is the joining of existence with quiddity, or spirit with body, by bringing into existence and formation. Then the Creator branches from the Speaking, since He gathers by saying “Be!”</p>
<p>In the third sense, His action consists in cutting off a measured portion of the rays of the unconditioned light of existence and attributing it to a cosmic reality by removing its unrestricted relation to nondelimitation. In this sense the Creator depends equally on the Powerful, Willing, Speaking, Knowing, Living, Generous, and Equitable; no such existential act can occur at all without the orientation, influence and judgment of them all.</p>
<p><strong>The Powerful</strong> (<em>al-Qādir</em>) possesses power, meaning the ability to produce an effect and perform an action at the moment of undertaking it. Before it is undertaken, however, this is an inward <strong>strength</strong> (<em>quwwa</em>). When it is conceived at the second rank in the measure appropriate to the judgment and relation belonging to it, and in accordance with what will has specified, it is called <strong>power</strong> (<em>qudra</em>). Power is outward, strength its inward reality.</p>
<p>The reality of power is that through which what is willed becomes manifest from knowledge into concrete actuality, without intermediary or causal means. Strength is that through which the powerful one finds himself able to determine what is willed, even though he has not yet undertaken it. <strong>The Strong</strong> (<em>al-Qawī</em>) thus belongs from one aspect among the names dependent on the Living, and in another aspect stands beyond it, as we explained in the second chapter.</p>
<p>Branches of the Powerful include <strong>the Firm</strong> (<em>al-Matīn</em>), who is independent and perfectly able to bear every—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p57" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p57"><h3 id="title-b2007-p57">B2007 p. 57 · The Originator, the Overpowering, and the Compeller</h3>

<p>—judgment and effect, and to give firm realization to every affair that is willed to appear through the concerted manifestation of the most beautiful names and their mutual support in the judgment of bringing into being and otherwise, in such a way that no weakness or defect can enter.</p>
<p>Among the names branching from the Powerful is <strong>the Originator</strong> (<em>al-Bāriʾ</em>), who is able to bring about an effect while giving exact attention to the determination, joining, and measuring performed, and to completing the inward preparedness to receive the form that <strong>the Fashioner</strong> (<em>al-Muṣawwir</em>) undertakes to disclose, in accordance with the determination of will and intention. This involves perfecting the plan, strengthening the parts and their sustaining principles, and giving the form its due. Thus the Creator determines all forms; the Originator provides the spiritual and imaginal forms; and the Fashioner the sensible forms.</p>
<p><strong>The Originator of the heavens and the earth</strong>, <strong>the Innovator</strong> and <strong>the Inventor</strong> mean the one who brings into existence <strong>without a previously given model</strong>—that is, without a model external to divine knowledge. For every existent is created according to a model already contained within eternal essential knowledge, which is not extracted from another or from anything outside itself, either originally or derivatively. This differs from human innovation and invention: all human knowledge is receptive and derived from what is external. These names accordingly depend from one perspective on the Knowing, and from another on the Powerful.</p>
<p><strong>The Overpowering</strong> (<em>al-Qahhār</em>) possesses complete efficacy and dominance over the outward and inward aspects of every affair, through elevation and causation. All besides God are conquered and overcome by His judgment as He prevails over them in successive states: existence and nonexistence; knowledge and ignorance; life and death; obedience and disobedience; graciousness and overpowering. He acts through and upon them until, in the end, His unity overcomes first their multiplicity of judgments and their imagined ownership, then their plurality of attributes, and finally their plurality of selves and determinations, through His one existence. This is the meaning of “To whom belongs sovereignty today? To God, the One, the Overpowering” (Qurʾān 40:16), and “He is the One, the Overpowering” (13:16). This name derives from the Powerful.</p>
<p><strong>The Compeller</strong> (<em>al-Jabbār</em>) restores things after alteration to their praiseworthy state through a kind of irresistible predominance and efficacy. The element of power and dominance entails reverent dread and greatness, whence <em>jabarūt</em>. The report, “Until the Compeller places His foot in it”—that is, Hell—and it says, “Enough, enough,” means that He sets it right and returns it by overpowering from its raging state to stillness, disclosing the greatness concealed within His mercy that prevails over anger—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p58" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p58"><h3 id="title-b2007-p58">B2007 p. 58 · The Compeller, Sovereign, Mighty, and All-powerful</h3>

<p>—exalted is He. It may be that “His foot” figuratively designates the <strong>last form</strong> among the forms of His perfect determinations and universal, all-comprehensive modes of manifestation—exalted and holy—for the foot is the final member of a form. This may concern fulfillment of the oath in “There is none among you but shall come to it” (Qurʾān 19:71), or the elimination of the most hidden remainder of relative deviating judgments arising at the extremities of His comprehensiveness from the detailed parts that compose the whole, or the granting of what is due to everyone by virtue of the perfection of true comprehensiveness. A similar meaning is suggested by the reported saying on Hell's behalf, “Pass, O believer, for your light has extinguished my flames.”</p>
<p>Understand this. The name Compeller in respect of majesty and reverent awe belongs among the names of the Living; in respect of restoration and rectification it belongs among those of the Powerful.</p>
<p>Another branch is <strong>the Sovereign</strong> (<em>al-Malik</em>), who possesses perfect prevalence, dominion and independent governance of His kingdom as He wills, preventing its members from oppressing one another, requiting each according to deeds—good with good and evil with evil—looking after their welfare, giving each what is due and securing it for them.</p>
<p>This world is the <strong>abode of causal means and intermediaries</strong> in all affairs. The attribution of judgments and effects to causes is outward, while the attribution to the One Who Causes Causes remains inward. The Real's exclusive sovereignty and independence are therefore concealed in this world, enabling creatures to claim a share in sovereignty or even independence in it.</p>
<p>The hereafter, however, is the abode of unveiling, where everything appears as it really is. His sovereignty therefore becomes evident, purified from all imagined participation, in the words “To whom belongs sovereignty today? To God, the One, the Overpowering” (Qurʾān 40:16). Thus His kingship is especially associated with the <strong>Day of Judgment</strong>, though no prevalence or sovereignty belongs to anyone but Him in either abode.</p>
<p>Branches of the Sovereign include <strong>the Mighty</strong> (<em>al-ʿAzīz</em>), the one who prevails against every opponent, against whom the defeated find no defense or escape; nothing can render Him incapable of enforcing any of His judgments, and He can be approached only through Himself.</p>
<p>Another branch is <strong>the All-powerful</strong> (<em>al-Muqtadir</em>), able to influence and act through causes and intermediaries, such as spirits and angels, analogous to a king's power exercised through soldiers and helpers. For this reason <em>Muqtadir</em> is joined with <em>Malīk</em> in “At a seat of truth, with a Sovereign All-powerful” (Qurʾān 54:55).</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p59" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p59"><h3 id="title-b2007-p59">B2007 p. 59 · The Majestic Sovereign and Owner of Sovereignty</h3>

<p>Among the names depending on <strong>the Sovereign</strong> is <strong>the Glorious</strong> (<em>al-Mājid</em>), who is the utmost limit of honor, kingship and extent of dominion, beyond which no increase is possible. Hence the authentic divine report says that when the servant recites “Master of the Day of Judgment” (Qurʾān 1:4), God replies, “My servant has glorified Me.”</p>
<p>Another dependent name is <strong>the Judge</strong> (<em>al-Ḥakam</em>), who decides between disputants, rightfully transferring to one what is in the possession of another, and who is able to satisfy the one against whom judgment is given because He controls the keys to outward and inward things. No other judge can necessarily satisfy both disputants. He alone is Sovereign, Judge and Just.</p>
<p>The Sovereign's branches also include <strong>the Governor</strong> (<em>al-Wālī</em>), who directly undertakes governance through all-encompassing knowledge, setting right the condition of those governed, judging accurately and making His judgment effective. No one can reverse His judgment or appeal against it.</p>
<p>Likewise <strong>the Supremely Exalted</strong> (<em>al-Mutaʿālī</em>) is He whose judgment cannot be overturned by any argument or contrary ruling supported by proof. Whoever attempts to repel His judgments by a proof finds his proof rendered void in opposition to His. He is exalted beyond every proof that would withstand His argument, or every judgment that would defeat His own.</p>
<p>Another dependent name is <strong>Owner of Sovereignty</strong> (<em>Mālik al-Mulk</em>). He owns the very selves of those whose affairs He administers and whose conditions He establishes. He governs them as an <strong>owner</strong> governs both outward and inward reality, unlike worldly kings, who rule only outward forms. All forms belong to Him, as do spirits and hearts. He owns His kingdom as He exercises sovereignty over His kingdom, disposing of hearts as He disposes of forms. This is alluded to in “Glory be to Him in whose hand is the <em>malakūt</em> of every thing” (Qurʾān 36:83).</p>
<p>Among these names is <strong>Possessor of Majesty</strong> (<em>Dhū al-Jalāl</em>), who possesses inward elevation, so that only whom He wills is chosen for nearness to Him. He is too majestic to be reached through striving or acquisition or for anything to be attributed to Him—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p60" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p60"><h3 id="title-b2007-p60">B2007 p. 60 · Descent and return, life and death, patience</h3>

<p>—in any respect. Thus He is present with creatures in every condition, existing in attribute yet separate in Essence.</p>
<p><strong>Possessor of Honor</strong> (<em>Dhū al-Ikrām</em>) is another dependent name: He manifests gentleness, blessing, and honor to His servants through bringing into existence, sustaining existence, setting affairs and states right, caring for welfare, and granting good recompense in this world and the next. God says, “For those who do good there is the most beautiful reward and an increase” (Qurʾān 10:26).</p>
<p>Among the names depending on the Powerful is <strong>the Initiator</strong> (<em>al-Mubdiʾ</em>). He manifests creation by causing it to descend from the world of power—of manifestation and hiddenness without intermediary—down toward the world of wisdom, where appearance proceeds through intermediaries and causes, stage after stage and rank after rank, crossing the ranks of deposit and settled residence until the attainment of mature age.</p>
<p>He then hands them over to <strong>the Restorer</strong> (<em>al-Muʿīd</em>), who returns creation, stage by stage, to the rank from which its descent began. God says, “God created you in weakness, then after weakness gave strength, then after strength gave weakness” (Qurʾān 30:54), and “As He began you, you shall return” (7:29). Every thing returns to the divine name from whose Presence its existence became first determined. The Restorer delivers it back to the name from which the Initiator first received that existence, under the rule of “God commands you to render trusts to those entitled to them” (4:58).</p>
<p>Other dependent names are <strong>the One Who Grants Honor</strong> and <strong>the One Who Humbles</strong> (<em>al-Muʿizz</em>, <em>al-Mudhill</em>). The former gives prevalence, strength and effective power to those prepared for it, to the highest degree of their competence and predominance. The latter lowers and abases those who deserve it by their reality, action, or acquisition.</p>
<p>Another branch is <strong>the Giver of Death</strong> (<em>al-Mumīt</em>), able to withdraw the means by which a thing attains its perfection, at the boundary where its completion has reached its appointed limit. The least of such cases is making the earth die in autumn; then the death of an animal; then that of the human being. Human death has several kinds: the bodily death caused by dying or being killed; the death of the heart through hardness, from the life of the original nature; and the death of the commanding soul through spiritual discipline, opposition, and struggle. In that last case the heart is brought to life with <strong>a life into which death can never enter</strong>.</p>
<p>Another dependent name is <strong>the Patient</strong> (<em>al-Ṣabūr</em>), whose perfect power enables Him to persist in bringing every thing undertaken to its completion without weariness or incapacity, and to grant respite to anyone opposing Him, though fully able to repel or remove him, so that proof and excuses may be completed against him.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p61" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p61"><h3 id="title-b2007-p61">B2007 p. 61 · The Generous, the Noble, the Forbearing, and the Forgiving</h3>

<p>As for the name <strong>the Generous</strong> (<em>al-Jawād</em>), it denotes the one who is able to give preference to others and actually bestows every perfection upon anyone deserving it through preparedness and state, or through request and petition.</p>
<p>Such bestowal occurs in seven kinds. <strong>First</strong>, by the gift of existence. <strong>Second</strong>, by the continuance of existence. <strong>Third</strong>, by the breathing forth of spirit and life. <strong>Fourth</strong>, by spiritual sustenance, such as guidance and faith and their degrees—repentance, renunciation and similar stations—knowledge and its degrees, and the gift to a servant of exalted character traits such as pardon, forbearance and mercy. <strong>Fifth</strong>, by making the effects of those character traits appear within him and treating him in accordance with them. <strong>Sixth</strong>, by the psychic sustenance of rank, eminence, dignity in both states of life, acceptance in people's hearts, and the like. <strong>Seventh</strong>, by bodily sustenance: enjoyable food, beautiful garments, fitting spouses, wealth, treasuries, stores and an agreeable life.</p>
<p>All these forms of giving are included within generosity and appear from the Generous, who can also perform excellently in bringing things into being, in speech and deed. What belongs especially to this name among these things is the initial gift of existence and excellence in the original act of bringing into being; the names branching from it participate in the other kinds, each being particular to one or more of them.</p>
<p><strong>The Noble</strong> (<em>al-Karīm</em>) is among the most comprehensive of its branches in judgment and effect. Nobility includes honor and eminence following the performance of good, relief of the distressed, and attainment of what merits praise, as in “A noble messenger came to them” (Qurʾān 44:17). It includes lofty station and distinction, as in “He prepared for them a noble reward” (33:44). It includes taking precedence in benevolence, pardon, overlooking wrongs, forbearance, forgiveness, and every kind of benefit, goodness and favor. One speaks of “noble land,” rich in plants, excellent pasture and sweet water without the toil of anyone; or says “His deeds are noble.” Nobility likewise embraces the skillful performance of every form of good and the assuming of worthy attributes in action and word, as in “The noblest of you before God is the most Godwary” (49:13).</p>
<p>The name Noble—exalted is His magnificence—therefore includes in its meanings all the meanings falling under the Generous, <strong>except the original bestowal of existence and continuance</strong> and the excellent fashioning of created things; those belong specially to the Generous.</p>
<p>Another dependent name is <strong>the Forbearing</strong> (<em>al-Ḥalīm</em>), who out of generosity refrains from taking a guilty servant to task although it is deserved, knowing the excuse of the servant's ignorant offense, and grants even a persistent offender respite for a wisdom and interest concealed from everyone but Him.</p>
<p>Another is <strong>the Much-forgiving</strong> (<em>al-Ghafūr</em>). The root meaning of <em>ghafr</em> is covering a thing to protect it from what would disgrace it. The Much-forgiving continually receives aid from its source, the Generous, so as to confer special mercy—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p62" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p62"><h3 id="title-b2007-p62">B2007 p. 62 · Forgiveness as merciful concealment</h3>

<p>—derived from the Presence of <em>al-Raḥīm</em>, covering the deviation called <strong>sin</strong> (<em>dhanb</em>) which has appeared in the servant from whom an evil or ugly action has issued. The word recalls the animal's tail (<em>dhanab</em>), the place where shameful parts may be exposed. Mercy thus protects the servant from the disgrace of the appearing consequence of the ugly action, whether sooner or later, in the form of pain, punishment, or the like.</p>
<p>Since creatures, through their selves, natures and the judgment of their possibility, are loci of defects, ugliness and evils, the Real continuously conceals what issues from them outwardly or inwardly, knowingly and intentionally or otherwise, by the effects of His mercy. These effects protect them against the consequences of what they do, whether reproach, blame, suffering or punishment, now or afterward.</p>
<p>For this reason the names most often occur in intensified forms: <strong>al-Ghaffār</strong> for the universality of repeated covering and <strong>al-Ghafūr</strong> for its many instances. One of the judgments of the universality of the Ever-forgiving (<em>al-Ghaffār</em>) is that He conceals from sinners His hidden overpowering power so that His wisdom may be completed; from the obedient He conceals His hidden bestowal of success by attributing acts, works and recompense to them in kindness; then from His friends He conceals all these so that they witness everything as a favor from Him. He covers from them the judgments of their own souls and even the effects of their createdness, so that they are realized through Him and appear through Him, not through themselves.</p>
<p>Another branch is <strong>the Pardoner</strong> (<em>al-ʿAfūw</em>), who through favor, generosity and concern refrains from holding a servant accountable for offense or injustice whose judgment and effects are evident to Him and others, obliterating the effect and judgment entirely or in most respects.</p>
<p>Another branch is <strong>the Compassionate</strong> (<em>al-Raʾūf</em>), who possesses the inward reality of mercy, tender-heartedness and kindness. Compassionate concern is the subtlest inward mercy proceeding from love and care; it inclines toward removing harms that the servant is too weak to bear and toward assisting him to attain desired things, benefits and things loved.</p>
<p>Another branch is <strong>the Ever-returning to Mercy</strong> (<em>al-Tawwāb</em>), who repeatedly returns with special mercy, pardon, forgiveness, care, success and acceptance of repentance after having turned away from servants during their repeated sins and violations, when their capacity to receive the effects of that mercy is absent or concealed. Thus, “They forgot God, so He forgot them” (Qurʾān 9:67), meaning that as they turned away from His remembrance in transgressing, their receptivity to His turning toward them disappeared, so He was as one who turned away—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p63" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p63"><h3 id="title-b2007-p63">B2007 p. 63 · The Bestower and the Opener throughout the ranks</h3>

<p>—from them. Shaykh Abū Madyan, may God be pleased with him, said, “The Ever-returning is the one who repeatedly returns to mercy; whenever you return, He returns.” [Farghānī then adduces a verse:] “From whichever direction the cup appeared, I stood to receive it.”</p>
<p>Another dependent name is <strong>the Bestower</strong> (<em>al-Wahhāb</em>), who gives initially, without reciprocal payment or recompense, so that the recipient owns the gift once it is received in the most fitting way. Its full realization can occur only in the paradisal life, or in a gift whose consequence endures there, such as faith and success in virtuous action. Everything else in worldly life is a <strong>trust or loan that must be returned</strong>, not something the recipient truly owns.</p>
<p>Another is <strong>the Opener</strong> (<em>al-Fattāḥ</em>), who first manifests goodness and amplitude after constriction and the closing of a gate. Opening is bringing goodness from the narrowness of hiddenness, revealing breadth and light from the constriction of the darkness of unarticulated unity.</p>
<p>The first manifestation of this name occurs when the forms of spirits are unfolded in detail within the Preserved Tablet, after having been restricted in comprehensive inclusion: “Nūn, by the Pen” (Qurʾān 68:1). It then opens <strong>imaginal forms</strong> from the matter of the universal dust (<em>al-habāʾ</em>); <strong>elemental forms</strong> from the same dust and the supreme element; <strong>mineral forms</strong> from the closure of their first joining and composition from the elements; <strong>plant forms</strong> from the constriction of their material basis; <strong>animal forms</strong> from the narrowness of their materials; and <strong>Adamic human forms</strong> from the constriction of the combination of water and earth.</p>
<p>It opens the receptivity of the womb or placenta of every female animal and human to the seed, after its prior closure. It opens the receptivity to animal or human form from the constriction of the embryonic lump. It opens the determination of the soul and the differentiation of its powers from the constriction of the undifferentiated source out of which its manifestation in the sensory world emerges to govern a balanced temperament. It opens the gate of birth and outward appearance in this world from the constriction of the mother's womb and the darkness of gestation.</p>
<p>It opens the gate of <strong>understanding and discrimination</strong> from the constriction of veiling; the gate of <strong>faith and Islam</strong> from ignorance and the judgments of divine favor; and the gate of intellect, knowledge, and inference from created product to Creator, from the constriction of the dominion of imagination.</p>
<p>Its most complete opening and the most widely beneficial in effect is opening the gate through which <strong>the heart is born from the constricted enclosure of the soul</strong>. Higher and more perfect still is the <strong>manifest opening</strong> (<em>al-fatḥ al-mubīn</em>): the opening of divine self-disclosure and unveiling of the lights of the Real from the constriction of the curtains of createdness. There belongs sainthood to the Real. Beyond this, what the attributes reveal and what remains concealed is more worthy and better in my view.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p64" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p64"><h3 id="title-b2007-p64">B2007 p. 64 · Sustenance, sufficiency, enrichment, benefit, and goodness</h3>

<p>Another dependent name is <strong>the Provider</strong> (<em>al-Razzāq</em>), who supplies every existent form with sustenance derived from that which constitutes its original formation. Spiritual forms are sustained through sciences and acts of witnessing; bodily forms through appropriate nourishment. Every sustenance operates according to its own character, sustaining the form to which it belongs, prolonging it according to the purpose for which it was created, and bringing it to its allotted completion.</p>
<p>Another is <strong>the Sustainer in Due Measure</strong> (<em>al-Muqīt</em>), who gives every existent exactly what suffices for its subsistence in nourishment and strength, neither deficient nor excessive. It falls under the Provider, who in turn depends on the Generous.</p>
<p>Another is <strong>the Rich or Self-sufficient</strong> (<em>al-Ghanī</em>) when the word signifies the possessor of wealth and sufficiency in the meanings of the essential, attributive and act-related names. In this respect He is rich through those names and their judgments and effects, bringing into manifestation whatever relates to all name-related perfections: “There is nothing whose treasuries are not with Us” (Qurʾān 15:21).</p>
<p>He is <strong>the Enricher</strong> (<em>al-Mughnī</em>) of any servants He wills, making those judgments and effects appear through and within them as existence, provision, continuance, knowledge, honor, nearness, eminence, bliss and all other things. Self-sufficiency and enrichment under this meaning thus branch from the Generous. But self-sufficiency understood as <strong>absence of any need whatsoever</strong> is among the negative essential names, not names of attributes.</p>
<p>Another dependent name is <strong>the Beneficial</strong> (<em>al-Nāfiʿ</em>), who brings repose and what suits hearts, spirits, souls and bodily natures, collectively or individually, in this world, the next, or both. His benefit to <strong>hearts</strong> is through self-disclosures and acts of witnessing; to <strong>spirits</strong>, through gnoses, knowledge, and unveilings; to <strong>souls</strong>, through the fulfillment of hopes and desires and attainment of pleasures imagined, understood, or known.</p>
<p>His benefit to <strong>natures and bodies</strong> comes through the kinds of sensible pleasure and comfort shared by animals: food, drink, clothing, sexual union, things seen, heard, and smelled. Some of these are mediated, others unmediated.</p>
<p>Another is <strong>the Benevolent</strong> (<em>al-Barr</em>), who conveys benefits to His creatures through graciousness, mercy and solicitude without seeking payment, return, or compensation for any right of service, worship or servanthood they might have, but through initiating mercy, kindness and compassion while they do not even recognize it. All these names branch from the Generous.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p65" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p65"><h3 id="title-b2007-p65">B2007 p. 65 · The Equitable preserves comprehensive unity; the universal Lord</h3>

<p><strong>The Equitable</strong> (<em>al-Muqsiṭ</em>) safeguards the comprehensiveness of all the names, together with that of the realities determining those names, whether original or derivative. Every name and reality among the roots and branches of the names and realities, down through their further branches, contains many further branches and gathers them into one. Indeed the very reality of the name is the <strong>comprehensive unity of its branches</strong>.</p>
<p>For instance, the name Generous and the reality of generosity comprehensively unite the Noble and nobility; the Much-forgiving and the Ever-forgiving and their realities; the Pardoner and pardon; the Compassionate and compassion; the Ever-returning and repentance; and the Opener, Bestower, Provider, Sustainer, Rich, Enricher, Beneficial and Benevolent, together with opening, bestowal, sustenance, nourishment, wealth, enrichment, benefit and goodness.</p>
<p>When one of these names or realities predominates and its judgment appears within that comprehensive unity, the influence of the Generous and the judgment of generosity remain concealed, while the influence of the prevailing name takes their place. <strong>What preserves the unity of the entire collection is the Equitable</strong>, together with its branch, the Just (<em>al-ʿAdl</em>).</p>
<p>Its preservation of comprehensive unity—in which the words for names and their meanings are included—extends to all roots, branches and ranks of the names and realities, and to all cosmic realities and ranks. It preserves their middle position between necessity and impossibility, and the intermediacy between them, indeed even the first intermediacy between <em>wāḥidiyya</em> and <em>aḥadiyya</em>. Nothing at all falls outside its judgment, just as no name falls outside the judgment of the Living and the perfection it contains.</p>
<p><strong>The Lord</strong> (<em>al-Rabb</em>) includes several meanings that share a single designation. One is <strong>owner</strong>, as one says “lord of the house” for its owner. Another is <strong>master</strong>, as in “He is my lord; he has given me a good lodging” (Qurʾān 12:23). Another is <strong>one who restores or sets right</strong>, as in an expression meaning to repair a well with pitch. Another is <strong>one close by who abides</strong>, as in the verb for remaining at a place. Another is <strong>one who nurtures</strong>, through blessings, sustaining assistance and undertaking what conduces to the well-being of those under his lordship—the commonest usage, as when one says “I raised the child.”</p>
<p>This name is therefore a <strong>universal name</strong>, pervading through all these meanings every universal and particular, original and derivative name down to its farthest branches, appearing within each in a manner appropriate to it. All cosmic realities depend upon divine realities—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p66" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p66"><h3 id="title-b2007-p66">B2007 p. 66 · The proper Lord of every determined reality</h3>

<p>—and arise from them, as we have explained. Whenever a person's human reality arises from some original divine reality, or any of its derivative realities through indefinitely many degrees of derivation, the existence ascribed to that person, appearing in spiritual, imaginal and sensory ranks, is determined from the Presence of a name whose determination is related to the divine reality from which the person's human reality came forth.</p>
<p>That name first determines the person's existence, through which he appears in the world of spirits. It thereafter continues supplying him with existence as he descends until he appears as a particular, sensible human individual. <strong>This name is his Lord</strong>, governing his nurturing and the setting right of his affairs and states. It is his Sovereign, Master, near and enduring companion, and the source of his existential assistance at every moment through <strong>continual new creation</strong> (<em>al-khalq al-jadīd</em>).</p>
<p>His point of return, final end, utmost aim and spiritual disclosures appropriate to his worldly conditions, together with his vision in the hereafter, pertain to that name and occur through it.</p>
<p>There is, however, a subtle distinction that must be noted. <strong>Lordship has two judgments: general and particular.</strong></p>
<p><strong>General Lordship</strong> occurs because the name <em>Allāh</em> has a general relation encompassing every world and rank and its inhabitants in both respects—the receptive reality and the existence appearing within it. Lordship attributed to <em>Allāh</em> is thus all-inclusive, as in “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” (Qurʾān 1:2) and “Your Lord is God” (7:54).</p>
<p>Likewise the name <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, having a universal relation through existence alone, has a general Lordship, as in “Your Lord is the All-merciful” (20:90). Every subordinate name is under the Lord of its principal name in the general judgment, not in the particular.</p>
<p>The <strong>particular judgment</strong> of Lordship is that every thing whose existence was first determined in the Presence of a name has that name as <strong>its proper Lord</strong>. Hence, according to Farghānī, scriptural reports of divine vision always speak of the vision of a Lord with a relation expressed: “Faces that day shall be radiant, gazing toward <strong>their Lord</strong>” (Qurʾān 75:22–23), and the Prophet's saying, “You shall see <strong>your Lord</strong>,” and analogous passages.</p>
<p>Thus the source from which the existences of perfected prophets, messengers and saints are drawn is the sea of the <strong>second self-disclosure</strong>, insofar as its second intermediary reality includes all the original principles, each of which contains the realities of all the others, but with a concealed trace of its particular distinction. The second self-disclosure, under this specifically distinguishing trace, is the Lord of that—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p67" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p67"><h3 id="title-b2007-p67">B2007 p. 67 · Muhammadan precedence and the image of converging seas</h3>

<p>—perfected individual. Those who approach the perfected among prophets, messengers and saints in receptivity, preparedness, comprehensiveness, universality, tasting and witnessing draw the source of their attributed existence from these same original principles, but insofar as their plurality, differentiation and particular effect are established, with a hidden trace of mutual inclusion rather than its complete reality, unlike the situation of the fully perfected. That name in its specific determination is the person's Lord.</p>
<p>Those below this rank draw their existence from <strong>branches of these seas</strong>, or from rivers branching from their branches, or from the rivulets of such rivers, channels, pools, jars and cups, down to indefinitely many drops. As their predisposition determines their first existence, so it determines their final return.</p>
<p>Our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, has <strong>the highest watering place</strong>: the first self-disclosure, which is first his Light and second his Lord. It is the original principle and source, beginning, point of return and final end of every name and of all determinations in knowledge and existence.</p>
<p>God says to him, “To your Lord is the utmost end” (Qurʾān 53:42), and “To your Lord is the return” (96:8). That is, every affair ends and returns to the first self-disclosure, which is your Light first and your Lord second. A similar meaning is indicated by “Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought another like it to replenish it” (18:109).</p>
<p>His Lord, whose words are inexhaustible, is the <strong>first self-disclosure</strong>, which is what the pronoun “He” signifies and what the inward reality of the name <em>Allāh</em> indicates. All divine and cosmic determinations of names and attributes necessarily return to this end, for God says, “To Him the whole affair returns” (11:123).</p>
<p>The <strong>words</strong> of this Lord are the essential names called the <strong>Keys of the Unseen</strong> and the realities indicated by pronominal names. These Keys are the principles of the seven leading names. The sea that is exhausted before such words are exhausted, and their inward foundation, is the <strong>sea of the second self-disclosure</strong>, from which the seven seas arise; these in turn give rise to rivers and rivulets whose determinations and words have no end in descent, and ascend again toward their origin.</p>
<p>The drops return to the cups, the cups to the jars, the jars to the pools, the pools to the channels, the channels to the rivulets, and the rivulets to the seas—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p68" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p68"><h3 id="title-b2007-p68">B2007 p. 68 · Overflow and return: the two directions of divine words</h3>

<p>—and the seven seas return to the sea of the second self-disclosure. They are exhausted and come to an end in returning to the <strong>first self-disclosure</strong>, the all-encompassing sea that is the drinking place of our Prophet Muḥammad, peace be upon him. The determination of this self-disclosure by its supreme names, which are its words, returns and comes to an end in the sea of <strong>nondelimitation</strong> and the innermost hidden pre-eternity.</p>
<p>As for “And were seven seas to replenish it, the words of God would not be exhausted” (Qurʾān 31:27), its meaning—God knows best—concerns <strong>descent</strong>, which realizes the perfection of disclosure. The sea replenished by seven others is the sea of existence, but considered as existence <strong>bestowed on and attributed to creatures</strong>, receiving from the seven seas of the seven original names as they turn toward descent and the completion of disclosure, through the manifestation of the judgments of names and realities at the cosmic ranks.</p>
<p>Existence, identical with the mercy embracing every thing and identical with <em>al-Raḥmān</em>, has <strong>two aspects</strong>. In the first, it bestows existence upon cosmic realities, disclosing the perfections relating to them. From it become determined divine names, principal and derivative, to each of which a judgment of bestowal is attributed, without any limit to their number, as we explained.</p>
<p>In the <strong>second</strong>, existence is itself bestowed and attributed to created beings within the cosmic ranks. Existential determinations arise from it, each attributed to a cosmic reality, some principal and some subordinate. All are God's <strong>words</strong> connected with His everlastingness, whose reality is the negation of finality. Consequently God's words in the descending direction, as connected with everlastingness, are inexhaustible.</p>
<p>In the direction of return, however, the bestowed determinations end in the branches of words proceeding from the Bestower: the names. Branches return to their origins; the origins return to the origin of origins, which is the <strong>Lord of Muḥammad</strong>, peace be upon him. The words of this gracious Lord are the Keys of the Unseen, ending in their inward reality, the eternal Presence, and the nondelimited hidden identity.</p>
<p>This is indicated by “To Him is the return of you all” (Qurʾān 10:4). For the letter <em>hāʾ</em> joined with <em>wāw</em> generally signifies the Essence considered through the outward Presence of Identity, whose comprehensiveness is indicated by <em>wāw</em>. Without <em>wāw</em> it signifies the Essence considered through pure real unity, the Unseen of the Unseen.</p>
<p><strong>Objection.</strong> You may say: “The particle <em>law</em> (‘if’) expresses the impossibility of one thing on account of the impossibility of another. This would imply that the sea's being exhausted is impossible because the sea's becoming ink for His words is impossible. But on your explanation both occur. How can this be reconciled?”</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p69" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p69"><h3 id="title-b2007-p69">B2007 p. 69 · Reply concerning the particle law and the two senses of the sea</h3>

<p><strong>I reply:</strong> We do not concede that the particle <em>law</em> expresses the impossibility of one thing merely because another is impossible. It can also express the occurrence of one thing because another occurs. Ibn Fāris says that <em>law</em> is a particle of supposition expressing the non-occurrence of something because another does not occur, <strong>and its occurrence because another occurs</strong>.</p>
<p>The Prophet—may God bless him and grant him peace—said, “The Qurʾān has an outward and an inward,” and so on in the report. Each possesses its own special meaning. Under the outward meaning, the verse indicates that the sea commonly understood in its evident sense would not be exhausted before the words of the Lord were exhausted: that common sea cannot become actual ink for visibly writing the Lord's words in an outward script.</p>
<p>Under the inward meaning, however, the particle <em>law</em> indicates occurrence on account of occurrence, just as we have explained. Understand and contemplate this difficult-to-attain chapter: you will acquire a treasure whose most precious jewels only the greatest among eminent men have obtained. God is the Self-sufficient, the Great, the Exalted.</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" data-part-start="Foundation II · Spirits" id="b2007-p70" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p70"><h3 id="title-b2007-p70">B2007 p. 70 · Second foundation: spirit and the world of malakūt</h3>

<p><strong>SECOND FOUNDATION: Concerning the judgments of the rank of spirits and the world of malakūt, and explaining how they are realized and determined from the Presence of jabarūt.</strong></p>
<p>Since the hiddenness metaphorically designated as a treasure precedes in rank the disclosure expressed by “that I might be known”—the final cause of which is the realization of perfection through the names—and since the <strong>original love</strong> expressed by “I loved” joins the two, demanding that disclosure which is the foundation and origin of the determination of the Keys of the Unseen and, indeed, all essential and attributive name-determinations, every thing that becomes determined or disclosed, appearing as a divine or cosmic name, an attribute, or a divine or cosmic reality, at any rank whatever of the Real or the cosmos, becomes determined and disclosed by that original love and its demand.</p>
<p>Original love pervades it and lies concealed inwardly within it. Whatever effect, judgment or orientation toward a perfection—whether conjectured or certain—is attributed to any thing whatever is attributed to it by reason of this permeation and inward presence. For no thing has an effect in another except by something inwardly present in it or proceeding from it. This is a foundation of the science of Reality.</p>
<p>Since original love has as its ultimate end and desired object the entire perfection of <strong>disclosure and self-vision</strong> (<em>jalāʾ wa-istijlāʾ</em>), and since the perfection of disclosure concerns the distinct appearance of the divine and cosmic names and attributes, their existential and intelligible differentiations, throughout all ranks and worlds of the Real and creation, nothing is devoid of the effect of love, passionate attachment, seeking and yearning. Their effects accordingly appear in diverse forms: hopes, desires, attachments, aims, purposes and thoughts. In each thing they appear according to its reality, the attribute prevailing over it and the judgment of its particular rank.</p>
<p>Thus, when the first determination and first disclosure, together with the Keys arising from it, had become realized; and thereafter the second determination, second intermediacy, and second self-disclosure were realized in the same manner; and the principal divine names emerged therein; and original love passed through the Keys into these principles and through them determined the remaining divine and cosmic name-branches, as explained in the preceding chapter—then the Keys manifested from within every divine name, attribute and reality according to its power of—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p71" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p71"><h3 id="title-b2007-p71">B2007 p. 71 · The second circuit of original love</h3>

<p>—causing an effect and performing the intended act; and from within every attributed cosmic reality according to its receptivity and preparedness. Original love emerged from the inward presence of the Keys pervading each of them in the form of seeking and yearning for the perfection concealed within it, whose manifestation in the ranks had been measured precisely for its disclosure. Thus existence, the world, the divine and cosmic names, attributes, and realities, principal and subordinate, became filled with seeking, love, desire, yearning, inclination and orientation toward perfection.</p>
<p>From the names this seeking was directed to the appearance of their requirements and objects: the disclosure of what is known, willed, empowered, created, provided for, and the like. From within the cosmic realities it arose as yearning for the overflowing of concrete existence so that their judgments and the perfections concealed within them might be displayed.</p>
<p>Every reality, through this seeking, yearning and supplication by its condition and preparedness, returns to the principle from which its determination issued, seeking aid from it and approaching through it to secure its objective. These requests and acts of recourse reach the <strong>seven principles</strong> on which the judgment and command to bring things into existence depend, and on which the satisfaction of the petitioners' needs and the success of their desired goal depend.</p>
<p>These seven principles, responding to such requesting, turn back from the Cloud-like Presence toward its interior, the very centre of the second intermediacy, its comprehensive aspect that determines the principles and contains them. Through their own seeking and yearning they also return to their origins—the Keys—awaiting a particular authorization. These return to the Presence of Identity and the inward reality of the name <em>Allāh</em>, which returns to the Unseen of the Unseen.</p>
<p>This is the <strong>second intelligible circuit of original love</strong>. Returning with authorization, it hastens downward, penetrating the Keys, then through them the inward reality of the principles, then their outward reality, then both sides of the second intermediacy and all the divine names within them to which influence and action are attributed.</p>
<p>It pervades also the cosmic realities to which being affected, undergoing change and receptivity belong. Thereupon their resurrection, as it were, occurred; their longing doubled and extended toward attaining what they had reached out their wings and necks to seek.</p>
<p>The name <strong>the Living</strong> rose to undertake the manifestation of universal governance and the presentation of the comprehensive affair, for the everlastingness of the original command to create. The name <strong>the Knowing</strong> came forward to articulate the details of that noble governance, presenting the particulars to which the judgment applies and the means completing the inevitable command. The name <strong>the Willing</strong> turned to order what the Knowing had differentiated within eternal knowledge, and to single out the reality of the Supreme Pen and the realities of the enraptured spirits for precedence in the command of witnessing and for readiness to receive the command—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p72" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p72"><h3 id="title-b2007-p72">B2007 p. 72 · The seven names and the first creation</h3>

<p>—to bring into being and to appear in the world of spirits <strong>without intermediary</strong>, while determining that the reality of the Preserved Tablet should receive existence <strong>through the mediation of the Pen</strong>, because of the strength of their connection.</p>
<p>The name <strong>the Speaking</strong> undertook to carry the judgment directly into effect by the word “Be,” because the other names are included within it and turn toward it. The name <strong>the Powerful</strong> prepared to display the effect of the Speaking through efficacy, attributing what <strong>the Generous</strong> pours forth from the source of mercy and generosity to the reality of the Pen and the enraptured spirits without intermediary, and to the Tablet and the spirits it contains through the mediation of the Pen. This is by setting the reality of the receiver opposite the ray of the Sun of existence.</p>
<p>The Generous hastened to pour forth existence so that the intended aim might be attained. <strong>The Equitable</strong> hurried to determine the locus and rank in which the created existent should appear, to establish intermediacy for each recipient that is to be witnessed, and to preserve the judgment of justice which assigns the middle position between necessity and impossibility.</p>
<p>Because the permeation of original love extended to both sides—existence, with the divine names determined from it to which influence and action belong; and knowledge, with its relations to knowable contingent realities which receive and undergo change—the issuing of the command “Be” and the receiving of “and it is” can only be attributed to the <strong>Keys</strong>. Yet between them lies the veil of the name Speaking, with the determination of the reality of the receiver from the Keys at the second rank. Thus the command proceeds from Him and returns to Him.</p>
<p>The first to receive the command to create <strong>without intermediary</strong> was the reality of the Supreme Pen, whose initial relation and manifestation to the first intermediacy, first self-disclosure, and affirmative essential names such as <strong>the One</strong> is stronger. At its rank stood the <strong>enraptured spirits</strong> (<em>al-arwāḥ al-muhayyamūn</em>), whose relation to the negative essential names such as <strong>the Unique</strong>, arising from the first disclosure, is even more fitting.</p>
<p>Then <strong>through the Pen</strong> came the reality of the Preserved Tablet, whose relation as a manifestation to the second determination, second intermediacy, second disclosure, and their differentiated judgments is stronger and more evident. The realization, determination and differentiation of all of these at the rank of spirits—their designation as Pen, enraptured spirits and Tablet, and the spiritual forms contained within the Tablet—and their being described as created and other arose through the conjunction of the existential share poured forth upon and attributed to their realities. This attribution results from their confrontation with that share in the Cloud-like Presence at the meeting and orientation of the names, outwardly or inwardly, as explained earlier, and from the reflection of the rays of that existential share upon the judgments of the determining realities whose judgments belong to the rank of spirits—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p73" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p73"><h3 id="title-b2007-p73">B2007 p. 73 · Reflection, divine freedom, and continuous renewal</h3>

<p>—such as the reality of the spirits' awe, simplicity, holiness and purity, and other such determinations attributed to creatures. The combined configuration arising from the bestowed rays and those judgments is called the Supreme Pen, the enraptured spirits and the Preserved Tablet. Their appearance with the realities they contain and their formation resemble the shape of a ray falling upon clear water and being reflected upon a polished wall. The water is an image of the receptive reality, and the polished wall an image of the rank. Understand: the example corresponds to the matter <strong>in some respects, not all</strong>. It is given to make the meaning familiar to one who remains veiled. The matter in its reality is subtler and simpler than all but a few of the great people of spiritual taste and understanding can grasp.</p>
<p>Recall, while considering what we have established, God's words: <strong>“Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shadow?”</strong> (Qurʾān 25:45). This means first the shadow of the essential names at the first rank from the very first self-disclosure, who is the Lord of Muḥammad, peace be upon him; then the extension of the shadow of the second determination, intermediacy and self-disclosure, with all their divine and cosmic names, attributes and realities, original and derivative, from the first determination, intermediacy and self-disclosure, because the latter contain the considerations of oneness and the essential names. Then He extends the shadow of the determinations of existence bestowed upon and attributed to created things, in the ranks of spirit, image and sense, from the outward aspect of all-merciful existence in its character as Bestower, to realize the complete perfection of the names.</p>
<p><strong>“Had He willed, He would have made it still”</strong> (25:45): that is, He could have kept the first and second shadows at rest instead of extending them through the cosmic ranks by the orientations and conjunctions of the names particular to this extension. The affair would still have been wholly complete with respect to Him, for <strong>He is independent of all worlds</strong>. Thus this extension occurs by <strong>will and choice</strong>, as indicated by “Had He willed,” <strong>not from the necessity of the Essence itself</strong>, as those whom Farghānī criticizes maintain.</p>
<p>“Then We made the sun an indication of it” (25:45) refers to the extension of the shadows, as in God's statement, “The highest similitude belongs to God” (Qurʾān 16:60). <strong>“Then We drew it back to Us in a gentle drawing”</strong> (25:46) means a drawing that is subtle, hidden and sublime, whose manner cannot be apprehended. This drawing resembles existence returning at every instant to its origin, since it is in truth an <strong>accident</strong>, and another like it arises in its place in <strong>new creation</strong>, as alluded to in “Yet they are in confusion about a new creation” (Qurʾān 50:15). It is analogous to nourishment and the oil in a lamp being dissolved from the body and lamp into the elements from which they emerged, while other sustenance replaces what is dissolved. All this occurs by the measure of the Mighty, Wise, Subtle and Knowing.</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p74" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p74"><h3 id="title-b2007-p74">B2007 p. 74 · Three aspects of the Supreme Pen and the two kinds of word</h3>

<p>Since the relation of the <strong>reality of the Supreme Pen</strong> to the first determination is the stronger—and unity, comprehensive inclusion and the concealment of differentiated considerations prevail there—the existence bestowed on it appears as one and comprehensive. Since the Preserved Tablet is more clearly related to the second determination, what reaches it through the Pen, in conformity with the command <strong>“Write My knowledge concerning My creatures until the Day of Resurrection,”</strong> becomes differentiated into two classes.</p>
<p>The first class is differentiated in the forms of <strong>words as acts</strong> (<em>kalimāt fiʿliyya</em>): the spiritual forms of all spirits and angels, indeed of the spirituality of every thing whatever. The second class appears as <strong>words of utterance</strong> (<em>kalimāt qawliyya</em>), such as the divine books and scrolls inscribed in it together in one act but sent down consecutively and separately to prophets and messengers. In reality they explain the states, affairs and measures of their judgments and their effects, in creation, word and deed. Each person understands of them according to his receptivity.</p>
<p>The Supreme Pen possesses <strong>three universal intelligible aspects</strong>. The first is that it receives existence and knowledge comprehensively and without intermediary, apprehending and recording what reaches it from the unseen Presence of its Originator. Under this aspect it is called the <strong>First Intellect</strong> (<em>al-ʿaql al-awwal</em>).</p>
<p>Its second aspect is the differentiation of what it receives comprehensively in the Preserved Tablet, under the command “Write My knowledge concerning My creatures,” or “Write what is to occur.” Under this aspect it is named the <strong>Supreme Pen</strong>. This aspect of it is the <strong>Muḥammadan soul</strong>, alluded to in the oath “By Him in whose hand is Muḥammad's soul.”</p>
<p>Its third aspect is its bearing the judgment of the first disclosure and being related to its manifestation in itself. In this consideration it is the reality of the <strong>Greatest Muḥammadan Spirit</strong> and his light, peace be upon him, under the aspect of—</p>

<p>The <strong>Preserved Tablet</strong> likewise possesses <strong>six universal intelligible aspects</strong>. The first is that it constitutes a collective configuration of the ray of bestowed and attributed light together with the judgments of quiddity pertaining to the world of spirits. This configuration comprehends both classes of the words-as-acts and words-as-utterances just mentioned—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p75" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p75"><h3 id="title-b2007-p75">B2007 p. 75 · Six aspects of the Preserved Tablet</h3>

<p>—fully differentiated, such that nothing entering existence up to the termination of the Day of Resurrection escapes it. In this respect it is called the [record of] <strong>every thing</strong>, intended by the Qurʾānic saying, “We wrote for him on the Tablets something of every thing” (Qurʾān 7:145).</p>
<p>Its <strong>second aspect</strong> is its orientation toward its Originator and reception of assistance from Him, in one of two modes. The first is <strong>without intermediary</strong>; in this consideration it is called a spirit attributed to the divine Presence and poured forth from the all-merciful Breath directly. From this spirit the spirits attributed to the perfected are breathed without intermediary, while the spirits of others are breathed through its partial spirit called an angel.</p>
<p>The other mode—which constitutes the <strong>third aspect</strong>—receives assistance through the Supreme Pen. Under this aspect it is called the <strong>Preserved Tablet</strong>.</p>
<p>Its <strong>fourth aspect</strong> is its descent and appearance insofar as part of what its reality and essence contain becomes separated and configured in that descent and appearance as simple and compound imaginal and sensory forms: Throne and Footstool, heavens and earths, and what lies between them, of angels, spheres, stars, elements and generated beings—mineral, plant, animal and human. This realizes the perfection of disclosure and self-vision. Under this consideration it is named <strong>the clear Book as act</strong>, intended in “There is nothing moist or dry but that it is in a clear Book” (Qurʾān 6:59) and “Ṭā-Sīn. These are the signs of the Qurʾān and a clear Book” (27:1).</p>
<p>Its <strong>fifth aspect</strong> is its orientation toward governing and perfecting what became differentiated from it and appeared as the imaginal and sensory existents described. It governs, preserves and perfects the universal in a universal mode, and the particular in a particular mode. Under this consideration it is called the <strong>Universal Soul</strong> (<em>al-nafs al-kulliyya</em>).</p>
<p>This aspect is directed toward governance in <strong>two forms</strong>. In the first, it governs in universal form; considered thus it is the soul of all prophets and saints except our Prophet, peace be upon him. For the rational soul governing his purified human form is the aspect through which the Supreme Pen differentiates what it received comprehensively and placed into the Preserved Tablet under the command “Write what is to occur.” It is alluded to in his oath, “By Him in whose hand is Muḥammad's soul.”</p>
<p>The <strong>second form</strong>, completing the <strong>sixth aspect</strong>, is the particular soul governing particular elemental individuals. Since the Preserved Tablet has these six aspects, the directions of the world branching from it number <strong>six</strong>: above and below, right and left, before and behind. Their <strong>seventh</strong> is the Tablet's comprehending all these aspects.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p76" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p76"><h3 id="title-b2007-p76">B2007 p. 76 · Four foundations and three complements of the creative names</h3>

<p><strong>Chapter.</strong> You have learned that the reality of the Preserved Tablet is more closely related to the second determination, called the <strong>rank of Divinity</strong>, while the Pen is more closely related to the first. Unity and comprehensiveness predominate in the first determination, and the same judgment predominates in the Pen; therefore the Pen receives the existence poured forth upon it only in comprehensive form. Because differentiation predominates in the second determination, the Preserved Tablet receives through the Pen that comprehensive existence in differentiated form.</p>
<p>The second determination or rank of Divinity has <strong>four pillars</strong> drawn from divine realities and <strong>three concomitants</strong> that complete and condition the full manifestation of its judgments and effects: these are the seven original leading names already identified.</p>
<p>Its <strong>four pillars</strong> are <strong>life, knowledge, will and power</strong>.
