It proceeds through a simple, undelimited orientation beyond restricting doctrinal conceptions, while affirming that the Real knows Himself in Himself by Himself, knows every thing, and that the Messenger of God knows and understands his Lord and what comes from Him. The entry into firmness, struggle, and enduring difficulty is included here.</p>
<p>Once repentance, holding fast and discipline have become <strong>firm dispositions</strong> of the soul through realizing what they contain, it becomes ready for the division of <strong>Gates</strong>, whose three principal stations are as follows.</p>
<p>First and most important is <strong>renunciation (zuhd)</strong>: leaving and turning away from what lies outside one's essence, beginning with outward accidents and objectives, then the inward forms of these, and thirdly everything other than the Real. Hope, aspiration and total devotion are included here.</p>
<p>Second is <strong>scrupulous restraint (waraʿ)</strong>: guarding against any matter in which there is a trace of deviation from revealed Law or a spiritually harmful ambiguity in whatever sustains one's sensible or intelligible form within this state of being. Contentment is included in it, and it is the form of Godwariness (<em>taqwā</em>).</p>
<p>Third is <strong>sorrow (ḥuzn)</strong> for perfections and their causes that have been missed. This comprises fear, caution, apprehension, humility and abasement before God.</p>
<p>When the soul has taken firm hold of these three, it becomes fit for the division of <strong>Transactions</strong>, in which one grants from the soul what belongs to its legitimate desires and takes from it what is due.</p>
<p>The most important and first station here is <strong>sincerity (ikhlāṣ)</strong>: purifying every inward or bodily act from every admixture. This includes refinement and rectitude.</p>
<p>The <strong>second</strong> is <strong>watchfulness (murāqaba)</strong>: constantly observing what one is directed toward, outwardly and inwardly. Care and reverence are included in it.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p129" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p129"><h3 id="title-b2007-p129">B2007 p. 129 · Entrustment and the initial disclosure of divine action</h3>

<p>The <strong>third</strong> station of Transactions is <strong>entrustment (tafwīḍ)</strong>: consigning every affair, before and after its occurrence, to the One who brings it about, knowing that He has greater knowledge of what benefits the person and is more merciful and compassionate toward him than he is toward himself. When it occurs <strong>through a cause</strong>, it is trust in God (<em>tawakkul</em>); when <strong>without cause</strong>, it is confidence (<em>thiqa</em>). In opposition to the jostling of intellect and imagination, it is surrender (<em>taslīm</em>).</p>
<p>When the soul realizes these stations while maintaining remembrance, gathering all its concerns and dismissing thoughts, the judgments of its veiling and the multiplicity of their effects begin to depart. Once multiplicity weakens in the soul, the effect of the unity of its gathering, hitherto concealed within the judgments of multiplicity, appears. This is a <strong>relative, partial heart</strong> belonging to the soul—not yet the <strong>true heart</strong>.</p>
<p>Its special <strong>sight and hearing</strong>, colored by the judgment of that unity and its equity, become apparent at the same time. With such sight the person sees whatever he looks upon as beautiful and good, and hears accordingly. Beauty and goodness signify the fitting relation among parts, colors and lights, and among attributes and character traits; they thus include the meaning of <strong>equilibrium</strong> and manifest the presence of the <strong>one divine act and attribute</strong>.</p>
<p>Ugliness, by contrast, manifests concealment of the effect of that unity under the predominance of multiplicity attributed to the object acted upon or described, not to the divine act or attribute in themselves, whether sensible or intelligible.</p>
<p>Through the <strong>heart's newly attained seeing</strong>, the traveler now becomes aware that the act of God is one and pervades every thing, bearing the characterization of beauty. This is the <strong>disclosure through acts (tajallī fiʿlī)</strong>.</p>
<p>At this station the person may experience a special loving inclination toward some beautiful <strong>human sensible form</strong>, the most encompassing manifestation of beauty, gentleness and perfection, when his sight is drawn toward it through affinity between divine action and the comprehensive relation. For the true Beloved, the Real, discloses Himself through His <strong>one act</strong> pervading all apparent causes and effects, in the mirror of the form being contemplated.</p>
<p>The person witnesses through that form a comprehending beauty and perfect loveliness which are the image of the one divine act, attributed to One transcendent of every particular restriction by an act or other quality. Disclosure by way of <strong>acts</strong> never takes place except through a manifestation, as explained earlier.</p>
<p>That manifestation becomes like a cup of love's drink, and the person's gaze conveys it to the mouth of the heart. Thereafter the judgment of love becomes general, because the witnessing of divine beauty in action extends to every sensible, intelligible and fashioned thing. Farghānī says that the point of entry and beginning of <strong>Ibn al-Fāriḍ's Tāʾiyya</strong>, whose commentary is the purpose of this work, lies at this—</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p130" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p130"><h3 id="title-b2007-p130">B2007 p. 130 · The soul's ascent and the spirit's estrangement</h3>

<p>—station. The proof is that the poem's love through acts ascends inwardly into <strong>love through attributes</strong>, and under its guidance and influence to the witnessing of the attributes, and beyond them to the highest stations. But we return to completing the exposition of the stations.</p>
<p>When the veils and the judgments of multiplicity described above, and their multiplicity, have been effaced from the seeker's soul through these <strong>three divisions and nine universal stations</strong>, and its unity appears, bringing about the kind of vision just described, the seeker moves from the station of <strong>Islam</strong>, which is like the pupil of the eye of faith, to its inward reality, which is like the <strong>light of that pupil</strong>.</p>
<p>As long as the human being remains manifest in this worldly constitution, the bond between <strong>soul, spirit and secret</strong> is very strong, yet each has a state of being proper to it.</p>
<p>The soul's state is <strong>sensible and witnessed</strong>, corresponding to the station of Islam. The spirit's state is a <strong>relative unseen cosmic rank</strong>, corresponding to the inward reality and secret of faith. The secret's state is the <strong>true unseen belonging to the Real</strong>, whose judgment is iḥsān.</p>
<p>The state proper to any one of these is a place of <strong>estrangement</strong> for the others. Whichever becomes manifest and predominates is at home, drawing the other two along as strangers within its own state.</p>
<p>The soul at the station of Islam has therefore drawn spirit and secret along with it in the journey of return to their Master and the path of arrival, through realization of those stations, removal of the soul's veils and witnessing of the act of its Lord.</p>
<p>When the journey of the soul is complete—its own unity manifest and the judgments of its multiplicity removed—the matter of traveling passes to the <strong>spirit</strong>, which must realize the truths of <strong>faith</strong> by removing concealed traces of distorted judgments remaining within the roots of character traits and qualities.</p>
<p>Their outward effects and branches had previously appeared in the soul and its faculties as deviation, multiplicity and contradiction, and were removed through discipline, repentance, renunciation, entrustment and the like. But a hidden remainder persists in the original roots belonging to the spirit, for the impression left on the mirror is itself affected by what had appeared in it. These remnants must be removed to perfect faith.</p>
<p>The spirit therefore enters upon its own journey, drawing the soul along in order to repel the prospect of evil, and drawing the secret along to seek benefit. The soul now experiences <strong>estrangement</strong>, so this degree of seeking is named <strong>Estrangement</strong> (<em>ghurba</em>), in reference to the saying attributed to the Prophet, “Seeking the Real is estrangement.”</p>
<p>For <strong>seeking</strong> that leads to <strong>finding</strong>, as in the saying that seeking and finding are twins, is only realized at this <strong>rank of faith</strong>. It has <strong>two pillars</strong>—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p131" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p131"><h3 id="title-b2007-p131">B2007 p. 131 · Patience, gratitude and contentment in the journey of the spirit</h3>

<p>Of the two pillars just mentioned, the first is the division of <strong>character traits</strong>, comparable to the conditions of prayer. The second is the division of <strong>fundamentals</strong>, by which I mean the roots of seeking that leads to finding, as we have said. These are comparable to the indispensable pillars of prayer.</p>
<p>The character trait most comprehensive in its judgment and widest in its effects is <strong>patience (ṣabr)</strong>, without which no affair is completed. Its reality is <strong>restraining the soul within obedience</strong> and keeping to the command and prohibition.</p>
<p>Patience also consists in refusing to contemplate one's own deeds and abandoning pretension, while demanding the same of the inward being; turning away from displaying knowledge, states and whatever experiences and secrets arise for the spirit; restraining spirit and secret from turmoil at every inspiration, incoming spiritual influence and divine disclosure, and remaining steady throughout.</p>
<p>Patience also applies to stations of affliction and ordeal, for the seeker sees them as removing the finest, most subtle <strong>luminous veils</strong>. Through such vision every trial and hardship becomes <strong>gift and favor</strong>. The seeker's task and station become gratitude where previously they were patience.</p>
<p>Thus patience extends its judgment over every station, character trait, deed and state. None of these can be realized without compelling the soul, whether followed or leading, to persevere in working toward them and to endure the difficulty of correcting and purifying them. Nothing falls outside patience.</p>
<p>The <strong>second pillar</strong> is <strong>gratitude (shukr)</strong>: first for the blessing of being created; second for guidance and the success that enables one to receive it; third for being supported in discharging the rights of the path; and fourth for reaching the rank of realization. Included within gratitude are truthfulness, humility, modesty, good character, preferring others, generosity and spiritual chivalry (<em>futuwwa</em>).</p>
<p>The <strong>third pillar</strong> is <strong>contentment (riḍā)</strong>. Its reality is that the seeker's soul, spirit and secret find everything appearing and occurring in existence, insofar as it issues from God's act, in conformity with what they will and love. They dislike nothing at all except what conflicts with <strong>revealed Law</strong>. They dislike and reject that through the law's language, in order to conform to it, not insofar as it is an act of God, the Wise and Knowing.</p>
<p>When this pillar is realized through these character traits, the burdens of the traveler become light and he enters earnestly upon his journey. In his pursuit of the desired object and arrival at the station of the Beloved he now resembles one who has crossed the deserts until the goal comes into sight. He is ready for the <strong>second pillar of the journey</strong>—the fundamental stations comparable to the pillars of prayer, which comprise <strong>four pillars</strong>.</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p132" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p132"><h3 id="title-b2007-p132">B2007 p. 132 · Intention, resolve, direct certainty and the certainty of reality</h3>

<p>The <strong>first</strong> is <strong>right intention (qaṣd ṣaḥīḥ)</strong> in one's orientation, based upon insight and tranquility through stripping away attachments and cutting off everything that obstructs the journey.</p>
<p>When one has formed this intention, a remnant of yearning and a slight glance back toward a trace of something from which one has separated may nonetheless overtake the traveler in the midst of striving. This remnant, still present within him, drags him backward even while the impulse to travel is strong. He must therefore strengthen that impulse by cutting off the remaining trace. This is called <strong>resolve (ʿazm)</strong>, the <strong>second</strong> pillar of the fundamentals.</p>
<p>These two pillars are strengthened by two things. <strong>Intention</strong> is strengthened by will, which impels the person to strenuous travel; <strong>resolve</strong> is strengthened by spiritual courtesy (<em>adab</em>), in which fear appears as <strong>contraction (qabḍ)</strong> and hope as <strong>expansion (basṭ)</strong>, while the traveler preserves an intermediate measure between the two.</p>
<p>Seeing that one's destination has drawn near produces an expansion of the share the seeker hopes to obtain from his goal, and intensifies his forward movement. Yet confronting the Presence of the Beloved and His majesty entails contraction, leading to hesitation and a slackening of the journey. Courtesy maintains equity between them and thereby strengthens resolve.</p>
<p>When resolve is sound, the veils of createdness grow thin, the traces of yearning and of glancing back toward dark cosmic judgments that produce ignorance and hesitation are cut off, and the judgment of the <strong>third pillar</strong> emerges: <strong>certainty (yaqīn)</strong> at its <strong>second rank</strong>, namely <strong>the eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqīn)</strong>.</p>
<p>This means tranquility and stability, dispensing with demonstrative proof because the reality of the thing is disclosed through <strong>witnessing the one divine act pervading every thing</strong>. It likewise dispenses with reports and faith in what was believed during the darkness of the unseen, because the star of direct witnessing of that act's own reality has risen.</p>
<p>The <strong>first rank of certainty</strong> is <strong>knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqīn)</strong>: repose and conviction concerning something unseen based upon the strength of its proof. It belongs to Islam and the beginning of faith while complete veiling still prevails.</p>
<p>The rank of <strong>reality of certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn)</strong>, however, pertains first to the breaking dawn of <strong>disclosures through attributes</strong>, and second to the rising of the sun of <strong>essential disclosure</strong> at the station of iḥsān. Included in the intermediate rank of certainty are intimacy and inward remembrance.</p>
<p>The connection of the eye of certainty to witnessing divine disclosure through acts occurring in a <strong>cosmic locus</strong> is indicated by “Then you shall see it with the eye of certainty” (Qurʾān 102:7), for seeing necessarily takes place through a manifestation.</p>
<p>When the traveler reaches this station, the <strong>spirit</strong> is freed from every bond of deviation or distracting orientation. Its unity and simplicity become manifest, distinct from the judgments of the soul and the multiplicity of the faculties and instruments through which the soul governs the body. The spirit's comprehensive unity, and the effect upon it of the disclosure of the <strong>one act</strong> attributed to the Presence of its Lord, become visible. The earlier struggle among <strong>secret, spirit and soul</strong> ceases, and the judgments of each rank become distinct. At that point the judgment of—</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p133" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p133"><h3 id="title-b2007-p133">B2007 p. 133 · Poverty and the reconciliation of spirit with soul</h3>

<p>—“My servant continues to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts until I love him,” comes into force. The One approached receives the approaching servant according to “If he comes to Me walking, I come to him running,” with effects of gracious solicitude <strong>until I love him</strong>.</p>
<p>At this point the traveler lays down the staff of his journey. The division of the hardships of his estrangement and of its veils comes to an end. The effects of divine love overtake him and transport him from the rank of createdness and separation to the Presence of protection and assistance.</p>
<p>He now realizes the truth of <strong>poverty (faqr)</strong>, the <strong>fourth pillar</strong> of the fundamentals. Its reality is being empty of every judgment of otherness—even of <strong>witnessing that emptiness</strong>, and even of negating the act of witnessing that emptiness. The word <em>faqr</em>, Farghānī explains through an etymological association with <em>qafr</em>, calls to mind an utterly barren land on which nothing grows or remains; the letters are regarded as transposed.</p>
<p>The attribution of agency belongs more strongly to the <strong>spiritual spirit</strong>, owing to its close connection with the Presence of Necessity and the appearance in it of the judgments of unity. The attribution of receptivity and being affected belongs more strongly to the <strong>human animal soul</strong>, owing to its connection with the Presence of Possibility and the appearance in it of plurality, one of its characteristic properties.</p>
<p>Each of the <strong>secret, spirit and soul</strong> has now witnessed that the display of its particular perfection depends on the other. The inclination toward perfection is a judgment rooted in each of them through the permeation of original essential love. Now that the effects of gracious care expressed by “until I love him” have appeared, that loving judgment moves each toward its partner.</p>
<p>The spiritual spirit, with its judgments, longs for the human soul like a <strong>contented husband longing for his faithful wife</strong>; the soul, with its judgments and original faculties, longs for the spirit like a <strong>contented, cherished wife longing for the husband who treats her well</strong>. Each inclines toward the other. They join together and intermingle with all that each contains of the unitary effects—</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p134" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p134"><h3 id="title-b2007-p134">B2007 p. 134 · Birth of the true heart and the first disclosures through attributes</h3>

<p>—and their balanced qualities, entering into <strong>another union in a different manner</strong>. From their conjunction, within the womb of the soul's comprehensiveness, is born a <strong>true heart</strong>, gathering all their judgments and also those of the secret, as an upright child devoted to both parents.</p>
<p>This comprehensive, unitary heart, Godwary and purified from the judgments of deviation, becomes the <strong>mirror and locus</strong> of the <strong>unitary disclosure through attributes</strong> determined from one of the Presences of the name <strong>the Outward (al-Ẓāhir)</strong>. The soul, with its faculties and instruments, had been the manifestation through which the complete disclosure and self-vision of that Presence appeared.</p>
<p>The judgment of this self-disclosure encompasses all its outward powers. The <strong>fourth inward depth</strong> of hearing, sight and speaking opens for the traveler, revealing that the faculties and attributes previously assigned to him in his veiled state had all, in reality, been attributed to the very disclosure insofar as it descended into the lowest ranks. Their attribution to his <strong>created nature</strong> had been figurative, not real.</p>
<p>The traveler now passes beyond all cosmic ranks and enters the beginning of the <strong>Presences of the Real</strong>, called the <strong>station of iḥsān</strong>. The reality of the authentic report becomes apparent: “When I love him, I become his hearing through which he hears, his sight through which he sees, his tongue through which he speaks,” and the remainder of the report.</p>
<p>Thereafter divine love raises him from the rank of one name to another <strong>higher in comprehensiveness and universality</strong>. It guides him through the valley of a quality and effect belonging to the divine names, the effects of which appear through and within him as knowledge, wisdom and insight belonging to the <strong>heart and its secret</strong>, not merely to rational or spiritual faculties.</p>
<p>He proceeds through the valley of <strong>discernment (firāsa)</strong>, in which his secret immediately grasps hidden matters that evade ordinary understanding, not by inference and deliberation. Then comes the valley of <strong>inspiration (ilhām)</strong> when his secret returns to the judgment of the manifestation and its veiling. Inspiration is a divine knowledge arriving at the heart, colored by the state predominant at that moment.</p>
<p>He then travels through the valley of the <strong>secret's tranquility</strong> after its agitation through awe and astonishment, effects of the majesty of the Unseen; then through the valley of <strong>repose (sakīna)</strong> arising amidst the wavering produced by such effects; then through the valley of <strong>high aspiration (himma)</strong> that stirs an intense rising toward sublime matters and their nondelimitation.</p>
<p>Once these valleys have been traversed, the judgment of this loving reality predominates outwardly over the traveler's secret. In accordance with <strong>“When I love him,”</strong> its specific properties, affairs and effects appear within his heart, secret, spirit and soul, some original and others dependent or derivative. These remove various hidden remainders of the restrictions peculiar to each of them through properties that the traveler himself does not perceive.</p>
<p>Indeed they remove even the <strong>very determination and qualification</strong> through which he is restricted, and the distinction attached to that determination—</p>

</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p135" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p135"><h3 id="title-b2007-p135">B2007 p. 135 · Eight successive states generated by love</h3>
<p>…and the effects of that restriction. Some of the realized masters designate the whole of these properties and effects of love as the <strong>division of states</strong> (<em>qism al-aḥwāl</em>).</p>
<p>The first is <strong>jealousy or protective exclusiveness</strong> (<em>ghayra</em>), which requires the removal of otherness (<em>ghayriyya</em>) and the shaking of the dust of the traces of createdness from the hems of the Real's reality.</p>
<p>Next is <strong>longing</strong> (<em>shawq</em>), an effect of jealousy: the stormy blasts of love's overpowering force arising from its intense inclination to join the one who longs with the object of longing, and the lover with the beloved.</p>
<p>Then comes <strong>agitation</strong> (<em>qalaq</em>): the effect of longing appears within the one who longs through intense disturbance and movement, issuing from a noncorporeal love directed toward removing the obstacle and intervening barrier—namely, the very determination of the lover and his distinctness through it.</p>
<p>Thereafter comes <strong>thirst</strong> (<em>ʿaṭash</em>), arising from this unsettling movement. It brings distress and burning that cannot be quenched save by a drop from the <em>Salsabīl</em> of divine care and existential assistance in the affair at hand.</p>
<p>Then the seeker's <strong>secret finds</strong> (<em>wijdān</em>) the pain and overpowering caused by that agitation and thirst, so intensely that it nearly causes him to become absent from his very determination.</p>
<p>Next comes <strong>bewildered rapture</strong> (<em>hayamān</em>), the actual realization of absence through the effect of ecstasy (<em>wajd</em>).</p>
<p>Then comes <strong>lightning</strong> (<em>barq</em>): a flash of nondelimited assistance arising upon that absence from the effect of determination, overpowering and wholly concealing the darkness of the latter's trace.</p>
<p>Finally comes <strong>taste</strong> (<em>dhawq</em>): the savoring of a drop of rain descending within that flash from the Cloud-like Presence, tending to allay the burning of the thirst mentioned.</p>
<p>These states elevate the traveler's secret and convey it from lower and more particular presences to higher and more comprehensive ones, relative to what is contained within the divine name <strong>the Outward</strong> (<em>al-Ẓāhir</em>). Its governing disclosure consists in the vision of existential unity within the multiplicity outwardly manifested through the soul and its faculties and instruments. Each state removes a limitation and determination particular to the presence from which the traveler is raised. With every restriction removed in these successive states, his secret gains strength, universality, power of apprehension, and proximity to the degrees of its final stations.</p>
<p>Some masters call this strengthening through a relationship approaching the final end <strong>the division of saintly powers or stations</strong> (<em>qism al-wilāyāt</em>). With that strength, the secret considers its own reality together with all its effects, original and accidental attributes and descriptions, and perfections obtained through or related to them. It also considers its relative or true final end, and the intelligible locus in which such consideration occurs. That locus is the inward dimension—</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p136" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p136"><h3 id="title-b2007-p136">B2007 p. 136 · The spiritual present, the secret, and the opening of stabilization</h3>
<p>—of time, called <strong>the moment</strong> (<em>al-waqt</em>) in the terminology of the Sufi masters: the state between past and future that possesses a certain permanence. All things known were related to it and established within it in the Presence of Knowledge. Each known thing belonged to an intelligible portion of it with all its appendages and concomitants; even the attribution of existence to those things was related to it.</p>
<p>Accordingly, the consideration undertaken by the traveler's secret also belongs to his <strong>moment</strong> and to what that moment requires. His state then becomes purified of the turbid admixtures of what is other. <strong>Consideration, the moment, and purity</strong> (<em>al-laḥẓ, al-waqt, al-ṣafāʾ</em>) are among his stations; he is thus clothed in <strong>joy</strong> (<em>surūr</em>) in his essence, his consideration, his moment, and his purity.</p>
<p>When he is established within a present state that is, relative to witnessing otherness, outside ordinary time, his condition is that of <strong>secrecy</strong> (<em>isrār</em>) under the judgment of the moment. No other person can become acquainted with him or his state. Farghānī alludes to the reported saying, “My friends are beneath My domes; none knows them apart from Me.” [Its prophetic attribution requires separate scrutiny.]</p>
<p>The saint who possesses this secret in this condition is master of <strong>one breath</strong>. Its effect appears in himself under the condition of his veiling and concealment, eliminating every form that occasions distance and obscuration and bringing forth one that entails disclosure, self-manifestation and nearness.</p>
<p>The effect may also appear according to his unveiled witnessing and self-disclosure, giving life to dead hearts, producing a form in one place and effacing it elsewhere. “I find the breath of the All-merciful coming from Yemen” points, on one reading, to the first state; “I shall bring it to you before your glance returns to you” (Qurʾān 27:40) points to the second.</p>
<p>One whose state is such remains a stranger among creatures. In bodily form he dwells with them; in meaning and inward secret he is apart from them. He has departed toward his homelands even while remaining outwardly settled among them in the place of his passing life. He is immersed in the vast sea of nearness, absent from the sensations of spirit, soul, and innermost intelligence.</p>
<p>He thereby enters the <strong>gate of stabilization</strong> (<em>tamkīn</em>) without being disturbed by <strong>variation</strong> (<em>talwīn</em>), meaning the changing self-disclosures of the outward divine names, in which the predominance of one name, together with its effects and judgments, alternates with that of another.</p>
<p>Both variation and stabilization manifest their effects and judgments at <strong>three ranks</strong>. At the first rank, that of outward disclosure, variation is the successive appearance in the traveler's heart and secret of the effects of different names, varying in judgments, changing in effects, and distinguishable by their attributes. Each particular disclosure veils him, through its special determination, from the operation of the others—until a flash of the all-comprehensive character—</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p137" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p137"><h3 id="title-b2007-p137">B2007 p. 137 · Stabilization within variation and the transition to the second journey</h3>
<p>—of the name <strong>the Outward</strong> appears and establishes him at the exact point of its middle or equilibrium, where the relationship of all names to it is equal. That point is the <strong>station of stabilization</strong>, whose occupant can realize any one of the names without being veiled from another by it.</p>
<p>The <strong>second rank</strong> is the rank of inward disclosure, whose judgments concerning variation and stabilization correspond to what we have just said concerning outward disclosure.</p>
<p>The <strong>third rank</strong> is the rank of comprehensiveness and intermediacy between the two—outward and inward. The individual judgments and effects belonging to each would otherwise entail concealment from those of the other. When the traveler occupies the intermediary between them he can <strong>comprehend and distinguish both</strong>, with no affair veiling him from another. This is <strong>stabilization within variation</strong> (<em>al-tamkīn fī al-talwīn</em>).</p>
<p>The stabilization just discussed earlier, however, referred to the <strong>first</strong> rank, that of outward disclosure. When the saint realizes its corresponding station, he begins the <strong>division of realities</strong> (<em>qism al-ḥaqāʾiq</em>). His first journey—the journey governed by love—has concluded with his realization of all the universal and particular names contained within the name the Outward. He now begins the <strong>second journey</strong>, the journey of the beloved, to witness the multiplicity of relational determinations belonging to inward affairs. Those affairs are a mirror for the unity of concrete existence, whose judgment predominates over the spiritual spirit.</p>
<p>For existence has, as we have said, <strong>two judgments</strong>: one insofar as it <strong>bestows</strong> existence (<em>mufīḍ</em>), the other insofar as existence is <strong>bestowed</strong> (<em>mufāḍ</em>). The first judgment predominantly affects the spirit, while the second affects the soul.</p>
<p>In the soul, the beam of concrete existence under the aspect of what is bestowed is a mirror for the multiplicity of judgments of cosmic realities associated with their ranks. That multiplicity is impressed upon the mirror of the single existential beam. Hence the reflected multiplicity is visible while the face of the mirror remains hidden, as happens with an ordinary mirror when a form is reflected in it.</p>
<p>In the spiritual spirit, by contrast, the multiplicity of relational affairs belonging to inward intelligible existence—whose images are cosmic realities—forms a mirror for the unity of outward concrete existence. <strong>Unity is visible there, while multiplicity remains inward and concealed.</strong></p>
<p>In the <strong>first journey</strong>, the veils constituted by the soul's judgments of multiplicity are lifted from the mirror of existential unity, until the unity of outward existence appears and is disclosed in the very multiplicity of the soul and the forms of the world. The perfection that descends from the One Existence and becomes manifest through that multiplicity is then disclosed.</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p138" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p138"><h3 id="title-b2007-p138">B2007 p. 138 · The reciprocal mirrors of outward and inward existence</h3>
<p>In the <strong>second journey</strong>, however, the traveler pierces the veil constituted by the unity of concrete existence, whose effects predominate in the spirit, so that the mirror of the multiplicity of relational affairs belonging to inward intelligible existence may be disclosed. Inward self-disclosure then appears with the special characteristics of that relational multiplicity: <strong>sciences of the Unseen and divine mysteries</strong>.</p>
<p>After the spirit is opened, its judgments belonging to its cosmic reality, its secret—by which Farghānī means concrete existence attributed to it—and its attributes undergo a mingling, action and reception analogous to what took place earlier between spirit and soul. Here, however, <strong>action is attributed to the secret</strong>, and <strong>reception to the spirit</strong>.</p>
<p>From the womb of the spirit there is thus born a <strong>heart</strong> capable of receiving inward existential self-disclosure. That disclosure contains the inward affairs and their relational multiplicity, with their manifestations, which are the intelligible forms. Through the journey across this inward Presence, the heart realizes the universals of the <strong>negative divine names</strong>. It enters upon the beginnings of inward self-disclosure in the division of realities, and the judgments of that division become manifest upon it, through it, and within it.</p>
<p>Know that the <strong>witness</strong> in this division is an <strong>outward existential secret</strong>, while the <strong>witnessed</strong> is an <strong>inward existential secret</strong>. The outward secret is a mirror for the inward secret, together with its judgments and effects; consequently the inward secret becomes manifest with those judgments and effects upon the outward secret, though its own reality and effects remain hidden from it. Indeed each is a mirror for the other under the judgment described. In their conjunction the reality and secret of everything become manifest as they are in the Presence of Eternal Knowledge, without alteration or substitution.</p>
<p>At first the inward secret appears to the outward secret from behind a thin veil of a divine or cosmic attribute or reality. It is also behind a transparent veil of a divine name qualified by a judgment belonging to a specific attribute. This is called <strong>unveiling</strong> (<em>mukāshafa</em>), since the reality of each is disclosed to the other with its judgment and description.</p>
<p>When each appears to the other <strong>without a manifestation of the reality of its attribute</strong>, but with an individual peculiarity and distinction through an intelligible secret included in each, the state is called <strong>witnessing</strong> (<em>mushāhada</em>).</p>
<p>When each directly beholds the other's very reality, with no attribute or particularity apart from this one's being outward and that one's inward, it is called <strong>direct vision</strong> (<em>muʿāyana</em>).</p>
<p>When each discloses itself to the other together with its own reality, attribute, and distinctive character, but the attribute no longer veils the reality itself, this is <strong>life</strong> pervading both of them, including the attribute and the particularity. It may be a knowledge, or a comprehensive affair between them, or a single existence that colors every relation with its own hue. Through this life each is protected from the death of the equilibrium of spiritual states, from the severing of this actual conjunction, and from the 'death' of absence from beginningless eternity.</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p139" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p139"><h3 id="title-b2007-p139">B2007 p. 139 · Contraction, expansion, annihilation within annihilation</h3>
<p>If unveiling, witnessing, direct vision, and life are <strong>restricted to the traveler himself</strong>, he is in <strong>contraction</strong> (<em>qabḍ</em>). If they expand from him so that another may attain them through his mediation, the traveler is in <strong>expansion</strong> (<em>basṭ</em>).</p>
<p>Contraction and expansion have another meaning. When his assistance in these matters comes from the <strong>majesty of the Unseen and its nondelimitation</strong>, the traveler is wrapped in contraction, to the extent that he is not free for apprehension or reflection at all. If the assistance comes from the aspect of <strong>beauty</strong>, he expands, appearing in a posture of intimacy and petition; he may become intoxicated by the strength of tasting and transgress his proper station, but when he becomes sober he repents. This is the highest station of repentance.</p>
<p>Assistance then continuously comes upon him and connects him with the One who supplies it. He subsequently becomes detached from the connections that still imply some manner of separation, and then from seeing either connection or separation, for both are [relative to his new station] one equilibrium.</p>
<p>All this belongs to the branches of the <strong>second rank of variation</strong>, and the judgment of determination continues to accompany them. This can cause each side to be veiled from the other when either becomes separate.</p>
<p>When the traveler reaches the end of this division and realizes its own station of <strong>stabilization</strong>, he transcends the station of inward disclosure and prepares to enter the <strong>Presence of the gathering of gatherings</strong> (<em>jamʿ al-jamʿ</em>). He has realized the reality of <strong>gnosis</strong> (<em>maʿrifa</em>), which comprehends the reality of the one known and knows what belongs to it and what stands against it. This is the beginning of the stations of <strong>final ends</strong>.</p>
<p>He now recognizes that something of the claims of <strong>annihilation within annihilation</strong> (<em>fanāʾ fī al-fanāʾ</em>) remains incumbent on him: removing restriction to the judgment of either one of the two disclosures, outward or inward, so that neither veils the other through its effects. He therefore turns with full determination to the Presence of the gathering of gatherings, seeking assistance from it through his receptivity.</p>
<p>Eternal solicitude then overtakes him: first through the <strong>annihilation of his knowledge</strong> restricted to one of the two disclosures; second through the <strong>annihilation of the specific determination and distinctness</strong> of each in the very Presence of the gathering of gatherings, which is their origin and source; third through <strong>annihilation from witnessing this very annihilation</strong>.</p>
<p>This occurs when the two names, Outward and Inward, display their specific perfections relating to the universals of their determinations, and return with those specific perfections and distinguishing judgments to the reality of the <strong>second determination and intermediacy</strong>. The intermediary exercises its rule over them through conjunction, mingling, activity, and reception. From their conjunction is born the reality of a <strong>vast, comprehensive heart</strong> uniting both Presences. This heart is the real image of the second intermediacy; the judgment of that annihilation then becomes manifest with the degrees already set forth. It is the <strong>annihilation of the particular reality in the particular reality</strong> (<em>fanāʾ al-ʿayn fī al-ʿayn</em>). From the rising place of this perfect and all-comprehensive heart dawns the sun of the <strong>essential, comprehensive, perfected self-disclosure</strong>.</p>

<p># Farghānī · Muntahā al-madārik — completion of the four foundations and the concluding preface ## New English working translation · Beirut B2007 pp. 140–145</p>
</section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p140" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p140"><h3 id="title-b2007-p140">B2007 p. 140 · The third rank of stabilization and the gathering of gatherings</h3>
<p>This second intermediacy, whose true image is the heart of the perfected one, is itself the <strong>Presence of perfection</strong> and its <strong>measure</strong>. It is the third rank of <strong>stabilization</strong> (<em>tamkīn</em>). Nothing remains upon him by way of name, trace, expression or indication to announce an actual separate determination or attribution.</p>
<p>There is nevertheless a concealed trace of the judgment of one of the original universal names. The spiritual traveler is now capable of <strong>assuming whichever garment he wishes</strong>, appearing in whichever locus of manifestation he wishes, and recognizing the One whom he knows in whatever garment He appears and whatever form He discloses, whether Real or creaturely. This is called the <strong>station of assuming garments</strong> (<em>maqām al-talbīs</em>). It stands above the stabilization that was termed <em>stabilization within variation</em>.</p>
<p>He thereafter realizes the reality of <strong>existence</strong>, which is that through which a determinate reality finds its intended object in every thing, by virtue of its pervasion of all that is called nonexistent and existent. Then he divests himself of all garments and loci of disclosure, witnessing and being witnessed with a heart that is <strong>absent yet present</strong>. This is the highest station of <strong>divestment</strong> (<em>tajrīd</em>).</p>
<p>He next becomes singular in seeing nothing except his own reality at the precise middle of the second intermediacy: the highest rank of <strong>singularization</strong> (<em>tafrīd</em>).</p>
<p>At that point he realizes the reconciliation of the <strong>negation of differentiation and its affirmation</strong>: seeing the comprehensive whole in its articulation and its articulation in the whole, throughout all the ranks of the Real and of creation. Thus the highest realization of tawḥīd is sound, as what is originated vanishes within what is beginningless, and otherness within the very reality.</p>
<p>The end returns to the beginning and completes the circle. He establishes public signs and testimonies for ordinary followers of revealed Law, rules and principles of guidance for the elect who follow the Path, and renewed gifts of divine care for the elect of the elect, the people of Reality. In this way all recognize by knowledge, direct vision, realization and its ultimate reality that <strong>the entire affair belongs to God</strong>: from Him it begins, in Him it ends, and to Him it returns. He is the First, the Last, the Outward, the Inward, and He knows every thing.</p>
<p>All this belongs to the states and stations of the Presence of <strong>“the distance of two bows”</strong> (<em>qāba qawsayn</em>).</p>
<p>The station <strong>“or nearer”</strong> (<em>aw adnā</em>), however, belongs especially to the journey of our Prophet Muḥammad, master of the first and last—upon him be peace—whose station the author of the poem undertook to interpret. The journey in that station begins only <strong>after the conclusion of all these stations</strong>. Its secret is <strong>witnessing every thing within every thing</strong>. Such a journey and witnessing arise through a conjunction and mingling between the essential names, including the Keys of the Unseen and their unitive judgments established at the first rank and attributed to the first self-disclosure, and the original universal names determined from the second self-disclosure after the manifestation of their particular perfections and their return bearing those perfections. The conjunction arises through original love, pervading the names and their spiritual and psychic manifestations.</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p141" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p141"><h3 id="title-b2007-p141">B2007 p. 141 · The Aḥmadian intermediacy and the Muḥammadan heart</h3>
<p>Through that conjunction and mingling, with the essential realities acting upon the attributive and the originals upon their derivatives, there is born a <strong>Godwary, pure, unitive, all-comprehensive Muḥammadan heart</strong>. This is the true image of the <strong>first intermediacy</strong>. Within it the <strong>first self-disclosure</strong> manifests itself. It possesses a unity encompassing all the universal and particular names, original and derivative, essential and attributive, <strong>without even the least predominance of one over another</strong>.</p>
<p>Thus in the traveler's spiritual taste, witnessing and vision through the eye of the heart, <strong>every name comprehends all the others</strong>. The expression <strong>“or nearer”</strong> alludes to this all-comprehensive unity.</p>
<p>Since original love, as we established at the outset, is identical with original receptivity, with the Aḥmadian <strong>Reality of Realities</strong>, and with the first intermediary between oneness (<em>wāḥidiyya</em>) and unicity (<em>aḥadiyya</em>), its orientation and attachment must be precisely to the <strong>Aḥmadian temperament and most equitable Muḥammadan heart</strong>—may God's blessings and peace be upon him.</p>
<p>These are the loci in which the first essential self-disclosure attains its complete self-vision at the rank of comprehensive unicity; this self-disclosure was, in the first instance, <strong>his light</strong>. It is for this reason that <strong>Beloved of God</strong> is among the Prophet's most distinctive titles.</p>
<p>The poet, having undertaken to interpret the Prophet's experience and journey through its stations, changes and stages, necessarily began his composition <strong>in the language of love</strong> appropriate to the Prophet and his reality.</p>
<p><strong>Love</strong> is the judgment of <strong>affinity</strong> (<em>munāsaba</em>), through which lover and beloved are connected. The kinds of affinity are restricted to <strong>five</strong>, and these return to two kinds referred to in verses attributed to Rābiʿa al-ʿAdawiyya:</p>
<blockquote>I love You with two loves: one born of desire,<br>and another because You are worthy of it.<br><br>In the love of desire, I remember You in secret until I see You;<br>in the love befitting You, remembrance of You consumes me from all besides You.<br><br>Neither love brings praise to me;<br>in both, the praise is Yours alone.</blockquote>
<p><em>The verse division and precise reading require collation against Rābiʿa's poetic transmission; the four English lines are a provisional rendering of the attributed verses, not a constituted critical text.</em></p>
<p>The <strong>love born of desire</strong>, he says, indicates <strong>essential affinity</strong> (<em>munāsaba dhātiyya</em>) for which no determining cause or origin is known. Therefore she said <strong>“Your remembrance in secret”</strong>, meaning God's remembrance of her.</p>
<p>The second kind of love admits four subdivisions. The complete enumeration is five, as follows.</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p142" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p142"><h3 id="title-b2007-p142">B2007 p. 142 · The five sorts of love, and disclosure through action</h3>
<p>Love and affinity are either related to the <strong>very Essence</strong>, without considering any additional meaning or attribute, or relate to the Essence as considered with some meaning or attribute beyond its very identity.</p>
<p>The <strong>first</strong> is <strong>essential affinity and love</strong> (<em>al-maḥabba al-dhātiyya</em>).</p>
<p>In the second case, either an effect from that meaning or attribute passes to another, or no such effect passes. If an effect does pass to another, this is <strong>affinity and love through acts</strong> (<em>al-munāsaba wa-l-maḥabba al-fiʿliyya</em>), as between a maker and the product of his work, or a writer and what he writes.</p>
<p>If no effect passes to another, either the attribute is stable and enduring in the one in whom it subsists or appears, or it is not. Where it is not stable, the result is <strong>affinity and love through states</strong> (<em>maḥabba ḥāliyya</em>), as between two people during a shared state of ecstasy or spiritual audition: the connection becomes apparent while the state lasts, and disappears when the state ends.</p>
<p>If the attribute is stable, it is asked whether, in the occurrence of the relation of love between lover and beloved, the judgment of the <strong>rank</strong> in which the meaning or attribute appears becomes dominant. If so, it is <strong>love through rank</strong> (<em>maḥabba martabiyya</em>), as between believers through faith or saints through sainthood—for example, those who love each other in the majesty of God.</p>
<p>If this rank-related judgment is not dominant, it is <strong>love through attribute</strong> (<em>maḥabba ṣifātiyya</em>), like other loves based on an enduring attribute.</p>
<p>Thus five kinds are distinguished. The classes of <strong>act, state and rank</strong> are reducible to the broader class of <strong>attribute</strong>; love through acts, in particular, is most readily recognized because the action's effects are conspicuous in its products. Hence the customary division of the divine names into <strong>names of the Essence, attributes, and acts</strong>.</p>
<p>For this reason the first self-disclosures that appear to the traveler are <strong>self-disclosures through acts</strong>. All things first appear beautiful and good to him. Through the majesty of that formal or intelligible beauty—which signifies unity and equity under the judgment of affinity and harmonious correspondence—he discerns the <strong>one act pervading every cause and intermediary</strong> through which agent, recipient and effect appear.</p>
<p>Love is then manifest through the comprehensive unity of the act connecting lover and beloved. This follows the disciplining and balancing of the soul's faculties and outward instruments through correct spiritual training and the observance of its conditions, or through original disposition and divine care, until the soul's veils become thin and transparent.</p>
<p>Thus in the poet whose work we are commenting upon, <strong>love and unification through action</strong> appeared first, as shown by his initial mention of vision within a <strong>sensible manifestation</strong>. At the beginning of the seeker's journey, such a vision occurs for the sake of making the reality familiar. Later, during outward self-disclosure, the locus itself is no longer seen: its appearance is eclipsed by the witnessing of the unity of the outward existential self-disclosure.</p>
<p>At the station of <strong>assuming garments</strong>, however, the one who has reached the end both sees and witnesses <strong>within and outside a manifestation</strong>. Because the poet relates the ascents and the path through the degrees of love, his first experience must be understood as vision through an act—</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p143" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p143"><h3 id="title-b2007-p143">B2007 p. 143 · Conclusion of the fourth foundation and transition to the poem</h3>
<p>—and <strong>not a vision of the very Essence</strong>. This becomes clear when we begin to set forth his ascents by commenting on the words and meanings of his poem, explaining the ranks and their foundations that are contained within it, bringing out what is deposited in its allusions, establishing the refinements of rhetorical art within its expressions, opening the locked places of its verses, resolving their difficulties, and developing what the poet states only comprehensively and in outline.</p>
<p>We shall undertake this, God willing, seeking help from Him, putting our trust in Him, and entreating Him in humility; confessing our shortcomings and negligence, drawing from the sea of His precious beneficence. For He is the best Patron and Helper. Praise belongs to Him for His favors, and blessings upon His Messenger Muḥammad, peace be upon him.</p>
<p><strong>The four foundations end here.</strong> B2007 pp.144–145 carry Farghānī's separate heading <strong>“Continuation of the preface”</strong> (<em>tatimmat al-dībāja</em>). These two pages belong to the introductory apparatus preceding the actual verse commentary; the authorial organizational distinction should be preserved in both Arabic and English.</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" data-part-start="Concluding preface" id="b2007-p144" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p144"><h3 id="title-b2007-p144">B2007 p. 144 · Continuation of the preface: four degrees of nearness</h3>
<p>A clarification of the matter intended, which is itself a preparation for beginning the promised commentary.</p>
<p>Know that the degrees of <strong>nearness</strong>—the final cause of spiritual journeying, the wayfaring of the soul and the removal of impediments, whether by divine care through attraction or by guidance through disciplined traveling—are restricted to <strong>four ranks</strong>.</p>
<p><strong>First</strong> is <strong>love</strong>, which may arise through attraction, as intended by the saying “My servant approaches Me through nothing dearer to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him,” or through disciplined spiritual traveling, as intended by “My servant continues to approach Me through supererogatory acts until I love him.”</p>
<p><strong>Second</strong> is <strong>tawḥīd</strong>, founded on love, as intended by “When I love him, I become his hearing, his sight and his tongue.”</p>
<p><strong>Third</strong> is <strong>gnosis</strong> (<em>maʿrifa</em>), founded on tawḥīd, as indicated by “Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, and through Me he understands.” The people of the Path call it the station of <strong>subsistence (baqāʾ)</strong>, <strong>gathering (jamʿ)</strong>, and <strong>Reality (ḥaqīqa)</strong>.</p>
<p><strong>Fourth</strong> is <strong>realization</strong> (<em>taḥqīq</em>). Under one aspect it is the station of <strong>vicegerency</strong>, and from every aspect the station of <strong>perfection</strong>. It includes all the previous ranks, joining beginning and end and their judgments; gathering and differentiation; unity and multiplicity; the Real and creation; qualification and nondelimitation. In this rank there is no clear predominance or subjection of one to the other: rather, presence without absence from any of them, and certainty without doubt.</p>
<p>We restrict the degrees of nearness to four because between the servant—possessing essential poverty and lowliness—and his Master—possessing essential sufficiency and dignity—there is a manifest separation which seems to exclude all relation or connection between them. <strong>Love</strong>, however, establishes and manifests between them—</p></section>
<section class="b2007-page" id="b2007-p145" aria-labelledby="title-b2007-p145"><h3 id="title-b2007-p145">B2007 p. 145 · Three aspects of the bond and the poem's itinerary</h3>
<p>—a <strong>relationship and connection in three respects</strong>.</p>
<p><strong>First</strong>, through the <strong>act</strong> that joins agent and recipient.</p>
<p><strong>Second</strong>, through the <strong>attribute</strong> forming the common measure between the one characterized by an attribute and what is so characterized, between what is eternal and what is originated, and between what is determined through itself and what is determined through another or incidentally.</p>
<p><strong>Third</strong>, through the <strong>Essence</strong>, which is identical with existence.</p>
<p>Love's subtle operation pervades first the act, second the attribute, and third the Essence. It removes the judgments of difference between agent and recipient of the action; then removes the accidental qualities, relations and metaphorical attributions attached to original attributes such as hearing and sight, until they are unified through the removal of such relations and attributions, as expressed in “I become his hearing and his sight.”</p>
<p>Then love leaves no other and no otherness, neither in reality nor in effect. Wherever love appears with sufficient intensity, <strong>tawḥīd</strong> follows; and through tawḥīd, <strong>gnosis</strong> is realized by the effect of the Beloved pervading the lover, as indicated by “Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he understands.”</p>
<p>Through return from beginning to end and the joining of their judgments, the rank of <strong>perfection and realization</strong> becomes manifest. Above that is the rank of <strong>supreme perfection</strong> (<em>akmaliyya</em>) proper to the Muḥammadan Presence, whose meaning the poet undertakes to interpret.</p>
<p>Because the matter is so, he began his poem with the rank of <strong>love</strong> and its stages for two reasons. First, love is the beginning of all the ranks of nearness, union and attainment of the intended goal. Second, beginning here signals the poet's role as interpreter of the possessor of the rank of supreme perfection, who has the station of love <strong>originally</strong>: the Prophet, may peace be upon him, was the target of the arrow signified by “I loved to be known.” Therefore he was the greatest of those who know God, and “Beloved of God” is among his most particular names.</p>
<p>The poet follows his exposition of the stages of love with the ranks of <strong>tawḥīd and gathering</strong>. There he returns to explanation and speaks in the language of guidance, mentioning the universal principles of the stations of spiritual wayfaring in summary.</p>
<p>Upon those ranks of tawḥīd he builds an exposition of the ranks and special properties of <strong>gnosis</strong>, followed by the ranks of <strong>perfection and realization</strong>. Most of those ranks he describes in terms of the pervasion of the judgment of the Muḥammadan station and its unitive comprehensiveness through every rank and every thing. He does so through narration and interpretation, as will gradually become apparent in the explanation of the verses, God willing.</p>
</section>
</article></main>

In the author's terminology, the three forms of annihilation are distinguished and are not to be reduced to a single vague statement about extinction.</li><li><strong>Textual standing (9 November 2026):</strong> This is a working translation of the remaining <strong>six printed pages</strong> of Farghānī's systematic introduction, using the <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic fourth-foundation transcription</a> which preserves B2007 page labels and clearly marks <strong>تتمة الديباجة</strong> on p.144. The Arabic has not yet been collated against the 1876 historical printing or medieval manuscripts. Printed page divisions do not necessarily correspond to authorial sentence divisions. Translation of the original <em>authorial introduction</em> now reaches its conclusion, but neither the English translation nor the underlying Arabic is yet a definitive critical edition. The subsequent verse-by-verse commentary is a separate workstream.</li></ul></li><li id="apparatus-p140"><a href="#b2007-p140">Beirut p.140</a> · <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic text, page 140</a></li><li id="apparatus-p141"><a href="#b2007-p141">Beirut p.141</a> · <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic text, page 141</a></li><li id="apparatus-p142"><a href="#b2007-p142">Beirut p.142</a> · <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic text, page 142</a></li><li id="apparatus-p143"><a href="#b2007-p143">Beirut p.143</a> · <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic text, page 143</a></li><li id="apparatus-p144"><a href="#b2007-p144">Beirut p.144</a> · <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic text, concluding preface</a></li><li id="apparatus-p145"><a href="#b2007-p145">Beirut p.145</a> · <a href="https://alshrefalm7sy.ahlamontada.com/t3214" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Arabic text, concluding preface</a><ul><li><strong>End of the concluding preface (B2007 p.145).</strong> The systematic introduction and its supplemental preface are now represented to their final known boundary in a continuous English working draft. The actual beginning of commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ's poem is a separate text division. Completion of this working English translation is NOT an independently constituted Arabic critical text, and no final critical-edition claim is made.</li></ul></li></ol></details></section>

### `full-reader.js`

<!-- BEGIN GNAMMA SOURCE full-reader.js SHA c5d4475d4e75cbf2e0d3a6a1a2f3e9f502f6a50a UTF8_BYTES 17099 -->
/* GNAMMA Farghānī introduction reader, Stage XVIII.
 * No text generation, source substitution, or silent modification of the translation.
 * Search indexes paragraph text in the static 128-page working English article. */
(() => {
  "use strict";
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const article = $("document");
  if (!article) return;
  const pages = [...article.querySelectorAll("section.b2007-page")];
  if (pages.length !== 128) {
    console.error("Farghānī reader: unexpected page count", pages.length);
    return;
  }
  const sections = pages.map((node, i) => ({
    page: i + 18,
    node,
    title: node.querySelector("h3")?.textContent || "Page " + (i+18),
    paras: [...node.querySelectorAll("p")]
  }));
  const last = sections.at(-1)?.page || 145;
  const foundations = [
    {name:"Foundation I · Essence and divine names",start:18,end:69},
    {name:"Foundation II · Spirits",start:70,end:78},
    {name:"Foundation III · Cosmos and Adam",start:79,end:101},
    {name:"Foundation IV · Human reality and return",start:102,end:143},
    {name:"Concluding preface",start:144,end:145}
  ];
  const storageKey = "gnamma-farghani-introduction-reading-v2";
  function readStored() { try { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(storageKey) || "{}") || {}; } catch (_) { return {}; } }
  const saved = readStored();
  const preferences = {
    scale: typeof saved.scale==="number" && Number.isFinite(saved.scale) ? Math.max(.85,Math.min(1.5,saved.scale)) : 1,
    theme: ["parchment","horizon","night"].includes(saved.theme) ? saved.theme : "parchment",
    wide: saved.wide === true,
    markers: saved.markers === true,
    bookmarks: Array.isArray(saved.bookmarks) ? [...new Set(saved.bookmarks.filter(n=>Number.isInteger(n)&&n>=18&&n<=145))] : [],
    lastPage: Number.isInteger(saved.lastPage)&&saved.lastPage>=18&&saved.lastPage<=145 ? saved.lastPage : 18
  };
  let current = 18, activeDialog = "", timer, ticking = false;
  const prefersReducedMotion = matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
  const motion = prefersReducedMotion ? "auto" : "smooth";
  const safeText = (tag, cls, label) => {
    const n = document.createElement(tag);
    if(cls)n.className=cls;
    if(label!==undefined)n.textContent=label;
    return n;
  };
  function persist() {
    try { localStorage.setItem(storageKey, JSON.stringify(preferences)); } catch (_) { /* Reader also works without storage. */ }
  }
  function toast(message) {
    const node=$("fr-toast");if(!node)return;
    node.textContent=message;node.classList.add("visible");
    clearTimeout(timer);timer=setTimeout(()=>node.classList.remove("visible"),2500);
  }
  function applyPreferences() {
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme=preferences.theme;
    document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--fr-scale",String(preferences.scale));
    document.body.classList.toggle("fr-wide",preferences.wide);
    document.body.classList.toggle("reader-clean",!preferences.markers);
    $("fr-theme").textContent="Theme: "+({parchment:"Paper",horizon:"Mist",night:"Night"})[preferences.theme];
    $("fr-wide").setAttribute("aria-pressed",String(preferences.wide));
    $("fr-markers").setAttribute("aria-pressed",String(preferences.markers));
    $("fr-markers").textContent=preferences.markers?"Hide page labels":"Page labels";
    $("fr-font-down").disabled=preferences.scale<=.85;
    $("fr-font-up").disabled=preferences.scale>=1.5;
    $("fr-font-down").title="Smaller text, current scale "+Math.round(preferences.scale*100)+"%";
    $("fr-font-up").title="Larger text, current scale "+Math.round(preferences.scale*100)+"%";
    persist();
  }
  function markCurrent(page, remember=true) {
    current=Math.min(last,Math.max(18,page));
    if(remember)preferences.lastPage=current;
    $("fr-current").textContent="p. "+current+" / "+last;
    $("fr-current").setAttribute("aria-label","Beirut 2007 printed page "+current+" of "+last);
    $("fr-prev").disabled=current<=18;
    $("fr-next").disabled=current>=last;
    $("fr-save").textContent=preferences.bookmarks.includes(current)?"★ Saved":"☆ Save";
    $("fr-save").setAttribute("aria-pressed",String(preferences.bookmarks.includes(current)));
    persist();
  }
  function progress() {
    // Track the position through the introduction, excluding the editorial apparatus.
    const start=article.getBoundingClientRect().top+scrollY;
    const end=start+article.offsetHeight;
    const value=end<=start?0:Math.max(0,Math.min(100,100*(scrollY+innerHeight*.35-start)/(end-start)));
    const bar=$("fr-progress-fill"),track=$("fr-progress-track");
    bar.style.width=value.toFixed(2)+"%";
    track.setAttribute("aria-valuenow",String(Math.round(value)));
    const y=innerHeight*.32;
    let candidate=18;
    for(const s of sections) {if(s.node.getBoundingClientRect().top<=y)candidate=s.page;else break;}
    if(candidate!==current)markCurrent(candidate);
  }
  function requestProgress() {
    if(!ticking){ticking=true;requestAnimationFrame(()=>{ticking=false;progress();});}
  }
  function closePanel() {
    const d=$("fr-panel");
    if(d.open)d.close();
    activeDialog="";
  }
  function panel(title,type) {
    activeDialog=type;
    $("fr-panel-title").textContent=title;
    const body=$("fr-panel-body");
    body.replaceChildren();
    const d=$("fr-panel");
    if(!d.open)d.showModal();
    return body;
  }
  function jump(page, target) {
    closePanel();
    const s=sections[page-18];if(!s)return;
    history.replaceState(null,"","#b2007-p"+page);
    const n=target||s.node;
    // Direct page/search jumps should not temporarily report intervening pages.
    // CSS may request smooth anchor scrolling, so use the explicit instant behavior here.
    n.scrollIntoView({behavior:"instant",block:target?"center":"start"});
    for(const x of pages)x.classList.remove("fr-target");
    s.node.classList.add("fr-target");
    markCurrent(page);
    // Target styling stays while navigating; never changes the content.
    requestProgress();
  }
  function resultButton(title,desc,onClick) {
    const b=safeText("button","fr-result");
    b.type="button";
    b.append(safeText("b",null,title));
    if(desc)b.append(safeText("small",null,desc));
    b.addEventListener("click",onClick);
    return b;
  }
  function input(label,placeholder) {
    const n=safeText("input","fr-input");
    n.type="search";n.placeholder=placeholder;n.setAttribute("aria-label",label);
    n.autocapitalize="off";n.autocomplete="off";return n;
  }
  function openContents() {
    const body=panel("Contents · four foundations","contents");
    const field=input("Filter the table of contents","Find a heading or page number…");
    const results=safeText("div");
    const help=safeText("p","fr-help","Jump to any of the 128 printed page labels. Page headings are navigation aids, not authorial divisions.");
    body.append(field,help,results);
    const render=()=>{
      results.replaceChildren();const q=field.value.toLocaleLowerCase().trim();
      let total=0;
      for(const f of foundations){
        const group=sections.filter(s=>s.page>=f.start&&s.page<=f.end&&(!q||s.title.toLocaleLowerCase().includes(q)||String(s.page).includes(q)||f.name.toLocaleLowerCase().includes(q)));
        if(!group.length)continue;
        results.append(safeText("h3","fr-foundation",f.name));
        const grid=safeText("div","fr-pages");
        for(const s of group){grid.append(resultButton("p. "+s.page,s.title.replace(/^B2007 p\.\s*\d+\s*·\s*/,""),()=>jump(s.page)));total++;}
        results.append(grid);
      }
      if(!total)results.append(safeText("p","fr-help","No matching printed-page headings."));
    };
    field.addEventListener("input",render);render();field.focus();
  }
  const searchData=sections.map(s=>({page:s.page,title:s.title,paragraphs:s.paras.map(node=>({node,text:node.textContent||""}))}));
  function normalize(t) {
    return String(t||"").normalize("NFKD").replace(/[\u0300-\u036f\u064b-\u065f]/g,"").toLocaleLowerCase();
  }
  function snippet(text,index,span) {
    const start=Math.max(0,index-65),end=Math.min(text.length,index+span+95);
    return (start?"…":"")+text.slice(start,end).replace(/\s+/g," ")+(end<text.length?"…":"");
  }
  function openSearch() {
    const body=panel("Search · complete English introduction","search");
    const field=input("Search the full translated introduction","Search for a word or phrase…");
    const hint=safeText("p","fr-help","Searches all 128 English page units; it does not search the separate Arabic excerpts or editorial notes.");
    const results=safeText("div","fr-results");
    body.append(field,hint,results);
    const render=()=>{
      const query=field.value.trim();results.replaceChildren();
      if(query.length<2){results.append(safeText("p","fr-help","Enter at least two characters to search."));return;}
      const q=normalize(query),matches=[];
      for(const p of searchData){
        for(const para of p.paragraphs){
          const index=normalize(para.text).indexOf(q);
          if(index>=0){matches.push({page:p.page,node:para.node,text:para.text,index});break;}
        }
      }
      hint.textContent=matches.length+" matching page"+(matches.length===1?"":"s")+" · showing up to 60";
      for(const x of matches.slice(0,60))results.append(resultButton("Beirut p. "+x.page,snippet(x.text,x.index,query.length),()=>jump(x.page,x.node)));
      if(!matches.length)results.append(safeText("p","fr-help","No matching passage found in the English working draft."));
    };
    field.addEventListener("input",render);render();field.focus();
  }
  function openBookmarks() {
    const body=panel("Saved reading places","bookmarks");
    const help=safeText("p","fr-help","Saved only in this browser. Bookmarks and your last page are not sent to a server.");
    body.append(help);
    body.append(resultButton("Resume at p. "+preferences.lastPage,"Last page reached in the introduction",()=>jump(preferences.lastPage)));
    for(const n of [...preferences.bookmarks].sort((a,b)=>a-b))
      body.append(resultButton("★ Beirut p. "+n,sections[n-18].title,()=>jump(n)));
    if(!preferences.bookmarks.length)body.append(safeText("p","fr-help","No saved pages yet. Select “Save” in the bottom reading bar."));
  }
  function openSources() {
    const body=panel("Source and textual apparatus · p. "+current,"sources");
    body.append(safeText("p","fr-help","The running English is a working translation. These links and notes provide the exact supplied source provenance; some later-page links lead to a derivative transcription, not a photographed printing."));
    const li=$("apparatus-p"+current);
    const div=safeText("div","fr-source-details");
    if(li){const clone=li.cloneNode(true);clone.removeAttribute("id");div.append(clone);}
    else div.append(safeText("p",null,"No source entry for this page."));
    const checking=safeText("a",null,"See selected bilingual source checks for page "+current);
    checking.href="critical-edition.html?page="+current;div.append(checking);
    body.append(div);
    const choose=safeText("button","fr-result");
    choose.type="button";choose.textContent="Browse sources for another page";
    choose.addEventListener("click",openContents);
    body.append(choose);
  }
  function openSettings() {
    const body=panel("Appearance & reading tools","settings");
    const root=safeText("div","fr-settings");
    const row=(heading,description,items)=>{
      const wrap=safeText("section","fr-setting-row");
      wrap.append(safeText("h3",null,heading),safeText("p",null,description));
      const actions=safeText("div","fr-setting-actions");
      for(const [label,action] of items){
        const btn=safeText("button",null,label);btn.type="button";
        btn.addEventListener("click",action);actions.append(btn);
      }
      wrap.append(actions);root.append(wrap);
    };
    row("Reading size","Current text size: "+Math.round(preferences.scale*100)+"%. Changes are saved in this browser.",[
      ["A− Smaller",()=>{$("fr-font-down").click();openSettings();}],
      ["A+ Larger",()=>{$("fr-font-up").click();openSettings();}]
    ]);
    row("Appearance","Change the page colors without altering any of the text.",[
      ["Paper",()=>{preferences.theme="parchment";applyPreferences();openSettings();}],
      ["Mist",()=>{preferences.theme="horizon";applyPreferences();openSettings();}],
      ["Night",()=>{preferences.theme="night";applyPreferences();openSettings();}]
    ]);
    row("Page layout","Printed-page labels remain optional; every page is still individually addressable.",[
      [preferences.wide?"Standard width":"Wide text",()=>{$("fr-wide").click();openSettings();}],
      [preferences.markers?"Hide page labels":"Show page labels",()=>{$("fr-markers").click();openSettings();}]
    ]);
    row("Reading and citations","Enter uninterrupted focus mode, copy the current source citation, or print.",[
      ["Focus reading",()=>focus(true)],
      ["Copy p. "+current+" citation",()=>copyCitation()],
      ["Print",()=>window.print()]
    ]);
    body.append(root);
  }
  async function copyCitation() {
    const title="Saʿīd al-Dīn al-Farghānī, Muntahā al-madārik, introduction, Beirut 2007 printed p. "+current+" (GNAMMA working English translation)";
    const url=new URL("continuous-translation.html#b2007-p"+current,location.href).href;
    const cite=title+". "+url;
    try {
      if(!navigator.clipboard?.writeText)throw new Error("No clipboard");
      await navigator.clipboard.writeText(cite);
      toast("Citation copied · p. "+current);
    } catch (_) { window.prompt("Copy citation",cite); }
  }
  function savePage() {
    if(preferences.bookmarks.includes(current))preferences.bookmarks=preferences.bookmarks.filter(n=>n!==current);
    else preferences.bookmarks.push(current);
    toast(preferences.bookmarks.includes(current)?"Saved p. "+current:"Removed p. "+current);
    markCurrent(current);
  }
  function focus(on) {
    document.body.classList.toggle("fr-focus",on);
    $("fr-focus").setAttribute("aria-pressed",String(on));
    if(on){closePanel();toast("Focus reading · Esc to exit");}
    requestProgress();
  }
  $("fr-contents-open").addEventListener("click",openContents);
  $("fr-search-open").addEventListener("click",openSearch);
  $("fr-bookmarks-open").addEventListener("click",openBookmarks);
  $("fr-source-open").addEventListener("click",openSources);
  $("fr-more-open").addEventListener("click",openSettings);
  $("fr-close").addEventListener("click",closePanel);
  $("fr-panel").addEventListener("close",()=>{activeDialog="";});
  $("fr-font-down").addEventListener("click",()=>{preferences.scale=Math.max(.85,Math.round((preferences.scale-.05)*100)/100);applyPreferences();requestProgress();});
  $("fr-font-up").addEventListener("click",()=>{preferences.scale=Math.min(1.5,Math.round((preferences.scale+.05)*100)/100);applyPreferences();requestProgress();});
  $("fr-theme").addEventListener("click",()=>{const all=["parchment","horizon","night"];preferences.theme=all[(all.indexOf(preferences.theme)+1)%all.length];applyPreferences();});
  $("fr-wide").addEventListener("click",()=>{preferences.wide=!preferences.wide;applyPreferences();requestProgress();});
  $("fr-markers").addEventListener("click",()=>{preferences.markers=!preferences.markers;applyPreferences();requestProgress();});
  $("fr-focus").addEventListener("click",()=>focus(!document.body.classList.contains("fr-focus")));
  $("fr-exit-focus").addEventListener("click",()=>focus(false));
  $("fr-print").addEventListener("click",()=>window.print());
  $("fr-prev").addEventListener("click",()=>jump(current-1));
  $("fr-next").addEventListener("click",()=>jump(current+1));
  $("fr-save").addEventListener("click",savePage);
  $("fr-copy").addEventListener("click",copyCitation);
  addEventListener("scroll",requestProgress,{passive:true});
  addEventListener("resize",requestProgress,{passive:true});
  addEventListener("hashchange",()=>{const match=location.hash.match(/^#b2007-p(\d+)$/);if(match)markCurrent(Number(match[1]));requestProgress();});
  document.addEventListener("keydown",ev=>{
    if(ev.key==="Escape" && document.body.classList.contains("fr-focus")){focus(false);return;}
    if($("fr-panel").open)return;
    const active=document.activeElement;
    if(active && /^(INPUT|TEXTAREA|SELECT)$/.test(active.tagName))return;
    if(ev.key==="/"||((ev.ctrlKey||ev.metaKey)&&ev.key.toLowerCase()==="k")){ev.preventDefault();openSearch();}
    if(ev.altKey && ev.key==="ArrowRight"){ev.preventDefault();jump(Math.min(last,current+1));}
    if(ev.altKey && ev.key==="ArrowLeft"){ev.preventDefault();jump(Math.max(18,current-1));}
  });
  document.documentElement.classList.add("fr-ready");
  applyPreferences();
  requestProgress();
  // Initial direct page anchor is respected. Returning visitors are offered Resume, never auto-scrolled.
  const hashMatch=location.hash.match(/^#b2007-p(\d+)$/);
  if(hashMatch)markCurrent(Number(hashMatch[1]));
  else markCurrent(18,false);
})();

<!-- END GNAMMA SOURCE full-reader.js -->

/* GNAMMA · Farghānī introduction · reading desk XVIII

.reading-toolbar{position:sticky;top:60px;z-index:23;background:var(--float);border-top:1px solid var(--line);border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);backdrop-filter:blur(16px);display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;justify-content:space-between;align-items:center;gap:5px 9px;padding:7px clamp(13px,3vw,32px)}

.fr-dialog::backdrop{background:#0e2125a6;backdrop-filter:blur(3px)}

.fr-dialog .fr-input{width:100%;padding:11px 13px;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:9px;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);font:15px ui-sans-serif,system-ui,sans-serif}
